title: No, Brian Eno Is Not Behind the Film Soundtrack for ‘At Night.’ Experimental Musician Elvin Brandhi Is.
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 8, 2026 2:40am 'At Night' In At Night , British filmmaker and artist Beatrice Gibson’s first feature-length film, the nightly sights and sounds of Paris interweave with the stories and conversations of six women – from hopes, dreams and sexual desires to worries about the future. Rhythm and mood are key elements that make the experimental and “autofictional” movie, which world-premieres on Saturday, Aug. 8, in the Filmmakers of the Present competition program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival , a special kind of cinematic ride. Just ask Locarno’s artistic director, Giona A. Nazzaro. In a chat with THR , he described the movie as “this nocturnal, ambient film where you can almost hear music that makes you think of Brian Eno . If At Night were a record, it could be music for lonely people at night.” Related Stories Movies 'Asphalt Guerrilla' Blends Fact, Fiction, AI and a Story About Filmmaking to Hold Up a Mirror to Our Time Movies Filmmaker Elham Ehsas Wants You to Know Afghanistan Sent a Man to Space in 1988 Written and directed by Gibson, At Night features cinematography by her long-time collaborator Ben Rivers and editing by Liyo Gong. But the music doesn’t come courtesy of Brian Eno. No, it is the creation of Elvin Brandhi. If you don’t follow experimental music, here are some basics to know about her. Elvin Brandhi is the pseudonym of Freya Edmondes, an improvising voice and sound artist who was born in Wales, but has become a citizen of the world. Her music features unusual beats created from field recordings, her own voice, tape, vinyl and instruments. She is also part of all sorts of music collaborations, including father/daughter “noise-improv berserkers” Yeah You, Pollution Opera with Nadah El Shazly, the duo Avril Spleen with Joseph Jadam, the band PFL with Peter Kutin and Lukas König, and the project Bahk with Daniel Blumberg. At Night , which features an array of Gibson’s non-professional actor friends and influences as they discuss and explore such topics as sexuality, money, motherhood and mental health, is the musical artist’s first-ever feature film soundtrack. And it seems fitting that she collaborated with Gibson on this film that press notes call “a love letter to friendships, relationships, and the quiet yet poignant stories women share together but rarely to an audience.” Brandhi took time out of her busy schedule to talk to THR about the creation of the soundtrack for At Night , her other music work and whether we may be able to hear more from her on future cinematic journeys. The artist confirms that the work on At Night marks a new step for her. “It’s the first time I’ve done a soundtrack for a feature film,” she tells THR . “I did a couple of short films with friends, and I make my own music video-type thing. So I consider myself more of an audiovisual artist. I think in both realms, but this was obviously very different. I’ve worked with Daniel Blumberg a little bit, hanging out with him a lot in the process of The Brutalist and then the Anne Lee film, [ The Testament of Ann Lee ]. I was doing quite a lot of vocal stuff, also with [avant-garde improvisational vocalists] Phil Minton and Maggie Nicols. And Daniel has been creating this nice bridge between the experimental scene in London and Hollywood cinema.” ‘At Night,’ courtesy of Night Films Courtesy of Night Films Ltd. So, this must be a good time for Brandhi to get her first feature film soundtrack under her belt, you may wonder. “It was probably helpful for me to get involved in the experience of how to make a soundtrack,” she confirms, but notes that it required a different focus from her usual work. “It was quite a unique experience, and I had to adjust a little bit how I think about composing. A lot of my music is quite in your face and trying to be as present as possible. But with a soundtrack, you have to almost make it sneak in from the sides, or be somehow invisible, coming out of the background.” Given that Brandhi works a lot with field recordings, how did the Paris setting of At Night play to her passions? “What was really nice about this film was that the metro is such a big center of the narrative, and that’s already quite a noisy place,” she tells THR . “It has a lot of the kind of frequencies and ambient noise and things that I might feel like field recording and be inspired by anyway. So it was this perfect entry point for coming into that film world.” Gibson and Brandhi have all sorts of connections but made their acquaintance by coincidence. “I met Beatrice for the first time at [the experimental music festival] Borealis [in Bergen, Norway], but only very briefly,” the music artist recalls. “We were in the same taxi going somewhere, and I was playing, and she was screening something. I think she knew of my music, and then a common friend, Leonardo Ruvolo, from Alcamo in Sicily, put us in contact because I also did his residency, and she’s living in Palermo [in Sicily] now, so there were various coincidences.” And the women quickly got along. “When we started working together, we became very good friends immediately,” Brandhi shares. “And working on At Night was a very intimate and special process.” But what was this process like, and how early did Brandhi start crafting music for the film? “Beatrice wanted to have as much sound as possible before even starting to shoot. So I did get sent a first draft of the script, but that did get changed as the film went through different shifts,” she recalls. “We spent a week going through ideas before any shoot. I sent her some drafts of things that might work. And she had one reference of a song that she really liked, which was actually from a collaboration I have that is called Insin [with Palestinian producer/MC Bashar Suleiman]. The track is called ‘Kidney Spears,’ which is a little bit more dreamy. I’m also singing in that. So I tried to send her other things within that kind of dynamic.” When Gibson started shooting in Paris, Brandhi also came to the French capital. “I was taking some recordings when they were going into the metro,” the musician tells THR . “And there was originally even a scene of me performing in Paris in the film.” ‘At Night,’ courtesy of Night Films Courtesy of Night Films Ltd. All in all, the soundtrack came together in an ongoing collaboration. “There were some core themes that we developed, and then little bits that needed a very specific kind of mood or dynamic,” she says. The collaboration also included editor Liyo Gong. “She is really amazing,” says Brandhi. “She’s also a DJ, so she has a very strong sense of the musicality in film and in how she edits.” Crystabel Riley also contributed, drum sounds, to the soundtrack. “I asked her if she would contribute some drumming that I could weave into different parts of it,” Brandhi recalls. “She was actually involved in the film, doing some of the makeup, because she’s a makeup artist as well as a musician.” Fans of the artist’s work may get to hear more from her in feature movies in the future. “I definitely would like to,” Brandhi tells THR . “I would be really up for it; it was really interesting entering the story and composing from a different perspective.” She adds: “I saw her playing live for the first time last year, and I was just so blown away because she’s such an incredible performer, and her stage energy is so engaging. There’s this warmth and tension as well. It feels very urgent. I was just watching her and felt the state of mind of the women in the film echoing in her performance.” Concludes Brandhi: “It was really special for me and Bea that she was part of it.” The creative mentions that she has also worked with video herself, and being involved with At Night inspired her to return to more of it. “In the lockdown, I did a lot more filming and editing stuff, so I feel that this soundtrack world is also a nice potential way to get back into the editing of my own film material,” she shares. Not that Brandhi doesn’t have all sorts of music stuff in the works. Including an album with Berlin-based Kenyan musician KMRU under their name A|||oy, which will be released on KMRU’s label offnot. “He is associated a bit more with ambient music. But we have so much in common and are both fans of each other’s music, even though it might seem like we have quite contrasting dynamics,” she tells THR . “There’s a strong similarity in the way we work with field recordings and sounds, textures and spaces.” Concludes Brandhi: “We’ve been collaborating for three years now, and we have an album coming out that we made between a couple of residencies, one at [Swedish electroacoustic music and sound art center] EMS in Stockholm, and then one in [Max Richter and his partner Yulia Mahr’s] Richter Mahr studio in Oxfordshire. We just listened to the test pressing, and it was really exciting. We’re both singing, and it’s completely different from both of our works.” THR

title: Satyajit Ray’s ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’ Making to be Chronicled in Srijit Mukherji’s ‘Maharaja Tomare Selam’
full_text: Aug 8, 2026 2:13am PT Satyajit Ray’s ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’ Making to be Chronicled in Srijit Mukherji’s ‘Maharaja Tomare Selam’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Male Contraceptive Doc ‘Give It a Shot’ From ‘Ask the Sexpert’ Director Vaishali Sinha Sets North American Theatrical Release, Unveils Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Vietnamese Boy Band Uprize Wants to Take Over the World: ‘We Won’t Set Limits for Ourselves’ 19 hours ago Danny DeVito-Produced Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Boards Blue Finch Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Indian National Award-winning filmmaker Srijit Mukherji is bringing to screen the making of Satyajit Ray ‘s “ Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne ,” one of Indian cinema’s most celebrated classics, in a new film titled “ Maharaja Tomare Selam .” Jeetu Kamal, Ritwik Bhowmik, Rudranil Ghosh, Satakshi Nandy, Sairity Banerjee and Arijit Dutta star in the film, produced by Hoichoi Studios and Friends Communication in association with Piyali Films Pvt. Ltd, the original producer of “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne.” Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale “Maharaja Tomare Selam,” which is also the title of a song in “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,” centers on Ray himself – the pressures he faced and the choices he made against the backdrop of a politically charged Kolkata – as he willed “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne” into existence. Principal photography will commence in January 2027. Popular on Variety Released on May 8, 1969, “Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne” followed two inept village musicians, played by Tapen Chatterjee and Rabi Ghosh, who are banished from their homes and granted magical powers by the King of Ghosts, which they use to avert a war between two rival kingdoms. Beneath the fantasy, the film carried social and political undertones around class and the role of art, a thread Ray sharpened into direct satire of authoritarian rule with his 1980 sequel, “Hirak Rajar Deshe.” His son, Sandip Ray, closed out the trilogy with “Goopy Bagha Phire Elo” in 1992. Ray built a body of work over more than three decades that includes “Pather Panchali” and “Charulata” among its landmarks. In 1992, weeks before his death, he received an honorary Academy Award for lifetime achievement, becoming the first Indian filmmaker so honored. “I am just trying to tell the incredible true story of how one of the greatest classics of Indian cinema, ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne,’ was conceived and made,” Mukherji said. Mukherji’s own credits include “Chotushkone,” for which he won the Indian National Film Award for best director, along with “Jaatishwar” and “Baishe Srabon.” He is known for his engagement with Bengali culture and storytelling, and with “Maharaja Tomare Selam,” he takes on a pivotal episode in the country’s film history. “Maharaja Tomare Selam” joins a run of Bengali films that have turned the camera on Ray’s own legacy. Anik Dutta’s “Aparajito” dramatized the making of “Pather Panchali,” with Kamal playing a character modeled on Ray, while Kaushik Ganguly’s “Apur Panchali” traced the later life of Subir Banerjee, the child actor who played Apu in that film. title: ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine
full_text: Aug 8, 2026 12:19am PT ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine German director Isabelle Stever brings sensitivity and visual ingenuity to this story of a young queer couple whose life together is upended by the Russian invasion. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine 2 hours ago ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller 1 day ago ‘Super Troopers 3’ Review: A Cult Comedy Franchise Seeks No Converts in Instantly Forgettable Third Go-Round 3 days ago See All 'I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming' Courtesy of X Filme Creative Pool GmbH Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine has prompted a wealth of urgent nonfiction filmmaking documenting the harsh realities of life under siege, but comparatively little dramatic storytelling — a space that the new German-Ukrainian production “ I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming ” occupies with bold formal imagination and a commitment to illuminating lives neglected in wider views of the conflict. A timely collaboration between German director Isabelle Stever and her wife, Ukrainian screenwriter Anna Melikova, the film is an intimate, bracingly intersectional relationship drama centered on a queer Kyiv couple whose attempts to flee to safety are complicated by local prejudice: a reminder that selective discrimination can still endure within a collectively persecuted population. Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Premiering in the main competition at Locarno, this is a warmer, more humane work than Stever’s last film, the coolly provocative 2022 incest drama “Grand Jeté.” If that film could travel, even securing U.S. distribution with Altered Innocence, there’s no reason to think “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” — with its topical subject matter and emotional accessibility, plus the imprimatur of producer Tom Tykwer — won’t gain wider exposure still. Paris-based outfit Outplay Films, which specializes in LGBTQ-themed titles, picked up the film for international sales shortly before its Locarno premiere; queer-oriented distributors and programmers will take particular interest in a work that would stand out for its candid depiction of transgender marriage even without its complicating wartime context. Popular on Variety What Stever’s latest shares with “Grand Jeté” is a crisp aesthetic rigor that some viewers may find distancing despite the immediacy of the drama, though it has ample sensory rewards. The director and DP Volodymyr Usyk (who shot the celebrated 2024 wartime doc “Songs of Slow Burning Earth”) rarely permit us a close, unobstructed view of their principal characters, Olya (Tania Myronyshena) and Oleh (Markus Bright), often shooting them from afar in slivered, reflective surfaces, over another person’s shoulder or through staggered doorways. Actually seeing these lives takes patience and some concentration; in the unforgiving world of the film, many choose not to. It opens on a conversation — viewed through a boxy apartment window at night, and later revisited on the other side of the glass — that finds Olya and Oleh’s longtime relationship at breaking point. “I entered a heterosexual relationship against my will,” Olya seethes to her partner. “You promised me you’d stay the same person.” Gradually, their history emerges: They met and got together as women in Kyiv’s small but throbbing queer scene, before Oleh came out as a trans man. That hasn’t weakened their bond; indeed, Olya even proposed marriage to him, to the surprise and delight of her conservative suburban family, who take it as given that their new in-law is cisgender. (Children are expected in short order; Olya tends to swerve the subject.) But Oleh’s transition did more or less coincide with the Russian invasion, which has severely hindered his ability to live freely and openly at a time when men are expected to serve their country in the armed forces. Medical certification of Oleh’s gender dysphoria cuts little ice with the military, who exercise institutional transphobia while taking him at his word regarding his identity. The couple’s plans to cross the border are thus mired in an absurdist tangle of administrative contradictions, and through the prism of Oleh’s impossible bind — in the eyes of the law, he’s at once recognized and rejected as the man he’s fought to be — Melikova’s script thoughtfully addresses how masculinity is defined and confined in the national psyche. Both non-professionals who bring a degree of lived experience to their characterizations, Myronyshena and Bright underplay effectively, communicating through finely expressive gestures and mirrored body language, and bringing an in-the-moment rawness to their frankly intimate, occasionally confrontational dialogue. “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” isn’t fashioned as a performance showcase, however: The actors often feel another dynamic element in Stever’s complex mise-en-scène, sometimes tellingly cramped in Usyk’s tight, stylized compositions, or muted in Andreas Hildebrandt’s hauntingly sparse sound design, which is given no score to contend with. There are passages of bravura technique here: One dazzling tracking shot spans the crowded, kinetic turmoil of the border in wartime, flooded with the red and blue lights of state authorities — visually redolent of neon-streaked queer club nights from the couple’s recent past, but a whole life away. A third-act development that again redefines the couple’s place in heteronormative society is somewhat rushed, leaning too heavily into melodrama to be wholly convincing. But it’s moving just the same, underlining the filmmakers’ interest in unorthodox found-family structures, and their foregrounding of minorities whose rights are often the first to be disregarded in times of national crisis. As the conflict in Ukraine trudges on, Stever’s stark, surprising film is a reminder that we’ve barely skimmed the surface of the country’s war stories. ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ Review: An Affecting Trans Relationship Drama Brings Fresh Perspective to the War in Ukraine Reviewed at Locarno Film Festival (Competition), Aug. 7, 2026. Producers: Uwe Schott, Tom Tykwer. Executive producers: Anna Melikova, Josef Reidinger. Co-producers: Natalia Libet, Olha Bregman. Crew: Director: Isabelle Stever. Screenplay: Anna Melikova. Camera: Volodymyr Usyk. Editors: Paul Groebel, Laura Lauzemis. With: Tania Myronyshena, Markus Bright, Iryna Mak, Viktor Zhdanov, Maiia Sobolevska, Maria Myronyshena, Oleksandr Rudynskyi. title: ‘Asphalt Guerrilla’ Blends Fact, Fiction, AI and a Story About Filmmaking to Hold Up a Mirror to Our Time
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 11:00pm 'Asphalt Guerrilla' Courtesy of Bando à Parte Real history, fiction and AI blend together for a look at a former radical far-left underground armed organization in Portugal in the new film from auteur Edgar Pêra ( Telepathic Letters , Manual of Evasion LX94 ), Asphalt Guerrilla ( Guerrilha no Asfalto ). The movie marks the Portuguese writer-director’s return to the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland, where it will world premiere in the Out of Competition program during its 79 th edition on Monday, Aug. 10. The militant group that the film revisits is the FP-25, short for Forças Populares 25 de Abril, or Popular Forces 25th of April, which was active between 1980 and 1987. It carried out dozens of bombings, shootings and bank robberies. The film is based on the eponymous book by Manuel Ricardo de Sousa, a member who ended up being lynched by a mob in the aftermath of a bank robbery. Related Stories Movies Denis Côté on Making 'Nobody's Violence,' His Assisted-Death Drama, While Fighting for His Own Life Music William Orbit, Grammy-Winning Producer for Madonna, Blur and Britney Spears, Dies at 69 But there is also a meta level to the movie. “It’s also about trying to make a film that ought to be shot in a guerrilla mode, with no compromises with the system,” notes the Locarno website. A synopsis teases the mind-bending quality of the movie by describing it as “a fictional film rooted in reality about a utopian time in Portuguese democracy.” And it continues: “Set in the early ’80s, it begins with a quiet student who becomes involved in a radical organization and ends up being shot and lynched by the mob in the aftermath of a bank robbery. Throughout the film, we witness the sometimes comical, sometimes tragic problems of these ‘asphalt guerrillas’ fighting against the system; at the same time, the director of the film quits the organization in order to fight to make films in a guerrilla mode.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte Pêra wrote the screenplay with Rodrigo Areias, and the voices of Pêra and Albano Jerónimo feature in Asphalt Guerrilla . Jorge Quintela is the cinematographer, while João Mora is the editor. The cast features Miguel Moreira, Maria Leite, Ivo Arroja, Jerónimo, Bernardo Santo Tirso and Luke Eberl. Pêra talked to THR about Asphalt Guerrilla , what inspired it and what it says about his latest take on the use of AI in filmmaking. “There are many films in this film,” Pêra highlights. “The very beginning was this book, which I read in the ’90s and basically shows a very amateurish group of guerrilla men or terrorists, depending on your point of view, but it gradually transforms into a film about my own guerrilla [film] scene, mainly because my friend and producer Rodrigo Areias made me do it.” Indeed, Pêra started making an underground name for himself in the mid-1980s with his avant-garde style as a “neuro-punk” filmmaker associated with DIY counterculture and the Portuguese music scene. “I would never pitch a film about me, including an autobiography, but I really understood that Rodrigo proposed it,” he tells THR . “I told him that I wanted the film to be about the future, not about the past, not about the ’80s and the problems we had back then in Portugal, but about this society and the state of cinema.” If you are watching the film and can’t quite tell which parts are real and which ones are fictional, Pêra won’t mind. “This fusion, or blur, of fiction and reality is something that I like, but it’s also something that I must fight against,” he explains. “So the film is also a mirror of what’s happening, where you sometimes don’t really know what’s real.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte Does he really feel like a film guerilla? “Actually, when I was in my 30s, there was this producer who called me the Sniper,” Pêra tells THR . “I think he said that with respect. I think I have that respect from other filmmakers of my country because I never tried to do anything that was not myself.” As the filmmaker did in his 2024 Locarno film Telepathic Letters ( Cartas Telepáticas ), Asphalt Guerrilla uses AI images. “I always try to leave some clues for what is AI-made,” he highlights. “But there are moments where, to show the danger of AI, you have to behave like a dangerous AI, which is why this film has moments [referencing] what worries me most, news becoming fabricated. And actually, the worst part is that AI also gets the most fun part of creating, such as [people] asking AI to write prompts.” Concludes Pêra: “So I try to fight all of that and create my own prompts and create my own algorithm. If you leave things to the YouTube algorithm, you know what you get.” Added the auteur: “You have to make at least a playlist so that you’re not invaded by this ultra commercial thing. That’s my fight inside of AI to create some images that are original in the way that they are recombinations of things that already exist. That’s what every artist does.” How does that fit into Pêra’s early neuro-punk days? “I was always interested in the effects of cinema on the minds of people and how the mind works,” he tells THR . “Neuro-punk was meant to say that we have to fight things with ideas, not with violence. So, cameras are weapons. Make films, not violence.” ‘Asphalt Guerrilla,’ courtesy of Bando à Parte The auteur didn’t necessarily know how timely his film would feel in a time full of wars, a rise in political and other radicalism and, of course, AI when he first started conceiving it. “I think it’s not a coincidence. It’s a synchronicity,” he offers. “But even when we think times are okay, we have lots of things that worry us. Now, we are in the worst of times, as they say. But even in the best of times, there’s still exploitation, people dying and all that. So yes, I think it’s a timely moment to go to the roots of the problems and not only focus on radicalism. I think radicalism is a symptom; it’s not the problem.” He sees the underlying issue this way: “Radicalism is a symptom of the decay of our system. I’m not an expert, but I feel that it’s not the radicalist we have to fight because that means [we are] becoming another radical. So that’s a trap. Instead, let’s talk about what makes our planet worse.” Pêra is working on another movie, which will keep speaking out about worries he has. It’s called The Spiral of Fear, and it’s about “big tech and what media says about the masters and all that.” THR

title: Taylor Swift Song ‘August’ Removed From Trump TikTok Video
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 10:13pm PT Taylor Swift Song ‘August’ Removed From Trump TikTok Video By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Taylor Swift Song ‘August’ Removed From Trump TikTok Video 4 hours ago Trump Nominates FCC Lawyer Danielle Thumann, an Adviser to Chairman Brendan Carr, to Serve as Commissioner 16 hours ago Don Lemon Asks Court to Drop Criminal Charges Against Him Related to Minnesota ICE Protest, Citing Donald Trump’s Chronic ‘Animus’ Toward Journalist 18 hours ago See All Getty Images A TikTok video that included Taylor Swift ‘s song “August” posted four days ago to the account for Donald Trump ‘s campaign has had the sound removed. The caption on the now Taylor-less “Team Trump” TikTok video reads, “I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august.” The video shows Donald and Melania Trump standing on a balcony watching fireworks with the text, “Mood because it’s August and Donald Trump is your president.” Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Fans noticed Friday evening that the Swift song, from her 2020 album “Folklore,” was removed from the Trump TikTok. In the U.S. version of the TikTok app, a message on the video reads: “The copyright owner hasn’t made this sound available in your country.” One of the top comments Friday on the video was from a user who said: “TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN.” Popular on Variety Variety has reached out to representatives for Swift and Trump for comment. The @TeamTrump TikTok account, which has 14 million followers, was set up ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election. It has continued to post videos regularly since Trump was elected for a second term. A Team Trump video that included Swift’s song “Father Figure,” posted Nov. 6, 2025, also has had the audio removed. However, one posted a day ago with a version of Swift’s “Red” still has the audio track available as of this writing. And a video on the official White House TikTok account from last November still is soundtracked with Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia.” In September 2024, Trump posted “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” on social media after the singer said she intended to vote for Kamala Harris for U.S. president . “I’m voting for @kamalaharris because she fights for the rights and causes I believe need a warrior to champion them,” Swift wrote in part in an Instagram post. title: Filmmaker Elham Ehsas Wants You to Know Afghanistan Sent a Man to Space in 1988
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 10:00pm 'Forgotten Spaceman' Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. In 1988, Afghanistan sent its first cosmonaut into space. Yes, really. Abdul Ahad Momand went where no Afghan had gone before — or has gone since — making Pashto the fourth language ever spoken beyond Earth. So why does barely anyone remember his name, his journey, or the hope it sparked among fellow Afghans at the time? Part of the answer may lie in timing: just as the spaceflight took place, Afghanistan was on the brink of civil war, a conflict that would soon force millions of its people into exile. As a new film argues, the country’s story has been shaped by conflict, exile and diaspora ever since, with science, culture and ideas pushed to the margins. Related Stories Movies Virginie Efira's Love for Cinema and Locarno Has No Limits -- Even If Her Mic Does Movies 'I Is Another' Review: Claes Bang Plays Himmler's Masseur in Weighty Meditation on a WWII Footnote Elham Ehsas ( There Will Come Soft Rains , Yellow , Our Kind of Love ), a London-based Afghan filmmaker and actor, is working to change that narrative and spotlight a piece of history too often left out of it. His short film Forgotten Spaceman — which blends documentary and essay elements while uncovering a surprising link between Afghanistan’s space history and his own family’s past — will world premiere on Aug. 9 in the Pardi di Domani – Concorso Internazionale program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival . Ehsas wrote, directed and edited Forgotten Spaceman , which is executive produced by Catherine Tschaepe and Jack Thomas-O’Brien of Ken Loach’s Sixteen Films, which backed the film. World sales and festivals are being handled by María Vera of Kino Rebelde. Beyond the story of Afghanistan’s spaceman and Ehsas’ own family history, the short also examines “shadows of colonialism and the memory of a fractured and silenced nation,” per its synopsis. Ehsas spoke with THR about his surprise at discovering Momand’s story, how Forgotten Spaceman came together, and what he hopes audiences take away from it. Can you share a little bit about the journey behind Forgotten Spaceman ? I feel this film was almost a coming of age for me in terms of getting to know my own past and my country’s past. I was researching a short fiction film that I was trying to make around space. And then I came across Abdul Ahad Momand, and I was like, “Who is this guy? How is it possible that we have an Afghan cosmonaut who went to space?” He put Afghanistan on the map in 1988. When he called his mom, Pashto became the fourth language ever spoken in space. It’s Russian, English, Mandarin and Pashto. And it just blew my mind. So I went to my parents and spoke to my mom and dad, and I was like: “How did you guys not tell me about him?” And it’s interesting because I’ve spoken to a lot of my cousins and family members my age and asked, “Do you guys know we have a spaceman?” And they were all [reacting the same way]: “What? Come again?” So, almost at every turn, this was a teaching opportunity for my own cousins and friends as well. It was such a discovery. And I also learned a lot. Through this experience of listening, I learned about making a documentary because it’s my first documentary. I learned to just relinquish control and go where this story is taking me. Sometimes, letting go is one of the best things you can do. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. The film starts out as a story about the Afghan spaceman, but then it also connects to your family story, and then you zoom out to show us a universal story. Did you know from the start that Forgotten Spaceman would also touch on these bigger themes? This whole film was a complete accident. I was trying to make this fiction film about space and then found Momand. And then I realized that he’s a refugee out in Europe somewhere, so then my idea was that I’d make a documentary about me looking for him. I put in about four, five months of work, shooting different footage around London. When I found out that he’s in Stuttgart in Germany, I thought I’ll go to Germany and speak to him. And then several months into this whole process, my dad gave me a picture. “Oh yeah, I have this photo of Momand.” That completely blew the whole thing open for me. It was insane. I can’t believe we have this photo, and I can’t believe that this photo speaks so much of my own family and of my own relationship with Momand and space, but also all of us and our relationship to home, to our country, to Afghanistan. Do you want to talk more about the photo and what it shows, or is that too much of a spoiler? And what did you do? I pivoted because I felt something was happening here. I am being guided by this film, and this film wants to be something else. Because I come from a narrative background, I’m used to scripting, casting, shooting, crafting, and engineering this whole narrative. But here is a true story that kept evolving, and it kept changing, and I felt the best thing here was to surrender to what’s happening. Maybe the story isn’t about me looking for Momand. Maybe the story is about this photo. And what if I can build something around this one photograph? No spoilers, but for people who see it, they’ll realize why this picture is so important, and that gave me the architecture for the rest of the film. Parts of the film felt a bit like a detective movie to me. And it also felt like a journey of discovery where another layer is uncovered. We see some family footage but also official, I assume, TV footage from Afghanistan about the space trip. Where did you find all this footage? It’s so interesting that you speak about the detective element. I almost felt like a detective trying to find this footage, these different pieces of archive. It’s really hard to find pre-Soviet era archive footage around Afghanistan, especially around such a niche as the space program. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy pf Foreigner Ltd. I reached out to a bunch of official, independent archive houses, [Russian Space Agency] Roscosmos, as well as the Afghanistan archive in Kabul. Because my dad is a journalist, he still has his network in Afghanistan. So I was speaking to a bunch of really interesting people, and through that, we found all of this beautiful footage. But I wanted the texture of the footage to not just be about his flight, but also about the rest of Afghanistan, about the history of his country. So that meant I had to dig deeper into the Soviet invasion from ‘79 to ‘89. At one point, I licensed about six hours of random footage that I didn’t know what it was. I just knew it was coming from Afghanistan and from that part of history. An archive house said, “Look, the deal is we’ll give you this for an affordable price, but we don’t know what’s in it, so you have to just take a blind shot.” So I had all of this footage, and it really helped me get the whole thing together. So, yes, the whole thing is a discovery. You have big-name executive producers on the film, such as Ken Loach’s Sixteen Films… I’m incredibly lucky for this project to attract such incredible collaborators, including someone like Ken Loach and Sixteen Films. They are renowned for telling stories that aren’t often told, telling human stories from different times and from different social and historical backgrounds. One of the executive producers is Sixteen’s Jack Thomas-O’Brien, who worked on this amazing film On Falling [by Laura Carreira]. So I have had a bunch of collaborators that I was sending the film to and getting their thoughts. The story started in my bedroom, and it just started getting bigger and bigger with all of these collaborators. It’s all about the magic of the moment [of the Afghan space trip], but also space and what it tells us about home and ourselves. I’m very lucky for the film to have resonated with incredible collaborators who have come on board and championed us and supported us. It’s just an incredible privilege and honor. You mentioned how Forgotten Spaceman goes into what space tells us about Afghanistan and, actually, also the exile experience. Can you talk about that a little bit? When I started this film, I thought I was making a film about this really super cool guy called Momand, who was an Afghan spaceman. But as the film was evolving in front of my eyes, I realized that there’s this family connection, so it’s also about me and my family. But then you keep going, and you keep discovering, digging deeper and deeper, excavating. And then I realized that actually this film isn’t just about Momand, me and my family. It’s about all of us and all of those people who have left home and moved. It’s about migration, it’s about refugeeship, it’s about the loss of home and the things we leave behind. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ director Elham Ehsas Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Here is Momand, an astronaut who went up to space, took the Quran with him and spoke Pashto up there. And then he came plummeting back down, went into exile, lived in Germany and became an accountant. So, it’s also about what a country loses when its children go into exile. That also speaks to memory, history and this divide between the East and the West. The East has these incredible stories, this incredible history, but this fragile memory, while the West has a short memory. As an Afghan filmmaker, I thought it was almost my duty to bring this story to life. I need more people to learn about Momand, and I need more people to know that he was Afghan. We’re not just bullets and blood and violence. We’re more than that. The West has chosen to only show Afghanistan in a specific light, which speaks to a bias. My colleagues from the diaspora and I feel it’s our duty to tell these stories in different ways. The film mentions that Afghans’ and Afghanistan’s stories usually get told through violence, conflict and war… Yes, for most of my lifetime, Afghanistan has been defined in the world’s imagination by conflict, headlines of war, statistics of death. But that’s not the country that my parents grew up in, or my grandparents. And it’s not the whole story of the place. Afghanistan is a country of poets and scientists and filmmakers and history and art and music, as I’ve shown in the film as well. And it’s a country that sent a man into space in 1988. When you start pulling on that thread, you find the whole landscape of achievement and imagination that has been buried and the tragedy of the lost potential of those people who had no choice but to move. Is that also why Forgotten Spaceman features Afghan music? I was faced with this incredible, epic tale of this man, and then through that tale, I zoom out and talk about our country and migration and refugees. But how do I tell that story, especially in a short documentary, in the most succinct way? I love music, especially Afghan music. I grew up on it, especially old folk songs. So, I thought, what if I engineer the film like a music album? What if it’s built around three different songs for the three different acts of the story? And that’s where the inspiration for that came. I went down this deep rabbit hole of old Afghan music that I grew up listening to, but also discovering new songs and remembering which songs my mum or dad used to listen to when I was a kid. I found these three beautiful, beautiful songs, and the fourth one in the credits by an incredible artist called Zarsanga. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. Does the film’s original title Hershewe Fazanawerd mean exactly the same as the English title – Forgotten Spaceman ? It literally translates to the man who went to space, or the spaceman. But Afghanistan has two national languages: Pashto and Dari. I was mindful that my previous films had dialogue in Dari, and I never included Pashto, which is actually my mother tongue, and it’s the language that Momand spoke in space. So, I decided to do the voiceover in Pashto, almost as an ode to my mother tongue and to Momand. I heard that you are working on your first feature as a writer and director? Yes, it’s a feature film called Our Kind of Love, and it’s based on my first-ever short film. We’ve been working hard on developing it with the BFI, and we’re just coming out of the script stage. Making films is so hard, and telling stories is so hard. I think there is value in putting a lot of time into trying to get it right, especially when you want to speak about a specific theme. Our Kind of Love ultimately is about the East and the West meeting. The short film was about an Afghan woman who was on a first date with an Afghan man who was born here [in the U.K.], and she was born in Kabul. It’s about how, if you put the East and the West together in a room, they interact. I’m a first-generation refugee. I came from Afghanistan to this country, and so I juggle two identities, and I juggle two cultures and countries. That’s what really always informs my work. ‘Forgotten Spaceman’ Courtesy of Foreigner Ltd. What’s next for Forgotten Spaceman ? We’re really excited that the film will premiere at the Locarno Film Festival , and then it is going to Toronto. I’ll be so curious being there for the first screening at Locarno to look at the audience and their reactions. It will be such a privilege for me to see them experience it. The film is how the legacy of Momand survives, and the legacy of these refugees who have done great things. Do you ever think that Forgotten Spaceman could be expanded into a feature-length film? Well, it’s such an epic story, and it’s such a beautiful story that speaks to so much. So, I’d be very curious to see and discover how it would look as a feature film. Is there anything else you’d like to highlight or mention? I want to also speak about my collaborators, the people I worked with on this film, and especially the music. My co-producer is Lorraine Bhattachary, and our composer CJ Mirra. Our sound designers are Rob Szeliga and John Cohen, who did such an incredible job because a lot of the film lives and dies in the sound. A lot of these experiences are so sonic, especially in space, and we wanted it to be something grand and beautiful. They all smashed it, and that’s what this film, and film in general, is about — collaboration. THR

full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All August 7, 2026 7:38pm Dwayne Johnson in Disney's live-action 'Moana.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Dwayne Johnson is speaking out on Disney ‘s live-action Moana not exactly being a hit with critics. Johnson, who voiced Maui in the original 2016 animated film Moana and its 2024 follow-up, recently spoke to People magazine about how the movie’s early reviews started positively before the reception shifted. “Our first two reviews came out. I’ll never forget it… They were amazing. I was like, wow,” the actor recalled, before adding that then “it went another way — as sometimes happens. That’s just the way it goes because we’re in this business.” Related Stories General News Former Walt Disney Imagineering President Bob Weis Signs With WME for Representation Movies Disney Admits 'The Mandalorian and Grogu' Disappointed at Box Office The Hollywood Reporter’s chief film critic, David Rooney, did, however, give the film a favorable review, calling it “one of Disney’s better live-action remakes.” He added, “The new Moana is a captivating family entertainment that deserves to find an audience.” The live-action Moana, released in theaters last month, earned a 31 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, while its audience score was significantly higher at 88 percent. The Smashing Machine star added that he and his wife, Lauren Hashian, had many conversations about the response. “The challenge was, OK, let’s remember, though, what’s going to be beyond this opening weekend. Let’s remember what’s happening right now and the noise that’s happening right now,” he said. “If you love it, great. If you don’t, no problem,” the Jumanji actor said. But what meant the most to him was that “the culture really stood up,” as Johnson is of Samoan heritage. “Because of me and our kids who can now look at the big screen and go, ‘That’s us for the first time on a big screen. That’s us up there. How cool is that?’,” he said. Catherine Laga’aia starred in the title role , taking over from Auliʻi Cravalho, who voiced the character in the animated films. Johnson reprised his role as Maui in the live-action adaptation. The film, though, didn’t make waves at the box office, grossing $264 million worldwide against a reported $250 million production budget . THR

title: Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 6:35pm PT Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup By Ethan Shanfeld Plus Icon Ethan Shanfeld @ethanshanfeld Latest Behind the Scenes of Obama’s Acting Cameo in ‘Life, Larry’: Blaming Larry David for His Tan Suit Debacle, Improvising Lines and Ranting About Ketchup 8 hours ago Jake T. Austin Opens Up About ‘Wizards of Waverly Place’ Revival Snub: I’m ‘Disappointed’ to Have ‘Not Been Included’ 19 hours ago Lala Sadii Disney Channel Series in Development 2 days ago See All Art Streiber / HBO In his HBO sketch series “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness,” Larry David travels throughout history, inserting his stubborn and curmudgeonly self into America’s most pivotal moments. “Lawrence,” as he’s often called, fights in the trenches of World War I, heckles George Washington during his Farewell Address and defends Rosa Parks on a Montgomery bus (for all the wrong reasons, of course). The show is produced by Barack Obama through his and Michelle Obama’s Higher Ground banner. So it’s only right that, in the series finale, Obama stepped in to reexamine the most historically important moment in his presidency. Not the killing of Osama bin Laden, the Iran Nuclear Deal or the legalization of same-sex marriage. No, something far more momentous and presidency-defining: the time he ignited a media firestorm by wearing a tan-colored suit to a 2014 press conference about ISIS. (The sartorial choice, which has its own Wikipedia page, saw Obama lambasted as “unpresidential,” was criticized by news outlets ranging from the New York Times to GQ to Fox News.) Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Obama appeared in the first episode of “Life, Larry” to help introduce the show. But when David and co-creator Jeff Schaffer told the former president they wanted him to act in a sketch, he and Higher Ground executive producer Ethan Lewis came up with the idea to relitigate the tan suit debacle. “From the very beginning, my dream was to close the book on the tan suit once and for all,” Lewis says. Popular on Variety Schaffer and David then devised a “Curb Your Enthusiasm”-like revisionist history in which David (appearing to play himself) is the one to blame for the fashion crime. In the sketch, Obama is preparing for the press conference while a mango smoothie sits on the Resolute Desk. When David asks for a sip, Obama turns him down to avoid “old lips” on his straw. When the president finally leaves the Oval Office, David goes to steal a sip of the smoothie, and he ends up spilling it all over the navy blue suit Obama planned to wear. When POTUS returns, David frantically tries to divert his attention away from the mess. “I think you should wear the tan suit to the press conference,” he says, insisting it’s “casual Friday.” Obama obliges, and tries on the lighter suit, causing David to deliver his classic, “prettay good… prettay… prettay… prettay… prettay good.” He assures Obama, “People are going to be talking about this for a long, long time.” Art Streiber / HBO Schaffer tells Variety that directing Obama was “one of the coolest things I’ve ever gotten the chance to do.” “It’s so cool being around him. You feel smarter and better, somehow, by just being in the area,” Schaffer says. “He had some great improv stuff. His comic timing was impeccable. He was a good actor, not just as a former president, but, like, as an actor.” Schaffer, who has worked with David since the “Seinfeld” days, was amused by watching Obama give the septuagenarian comedian notes. “The funny thing was watching him go, ‘Larry, you’re coming in late!’ He was the president, so he’s used to telling people what to do. Larry was in the odd position of being told what to do, which never happens on a Larry set.” The most nerve-wracking part of directing a former president? “The first thing was: What do I call this man?” Schaffer says. “I’m directing and things are moving fast, and I have to remember, ‘Sir, let’s do that one more time.’ Or, ‘Hold on, Mr. President.’ I didn’t want to screw things up and go, ‘Hey, Barack.’” The Oval Office stage was crafted by the Obamas’ interior designer Michael S. Smith, who led the 2010 makeover of the real White House room. Smith perfected the layout and furniture of the space, so much so that when Obama walked in, he said, “This is unbelievable. It looks just like it was when I was here,” Schaffer remembers. The attention to detail extended even to Obama’s on-screen aide, played by his real-life Director of Oval Office Operations Brian Mosteller. According to Schaffer, just as surreal as directing the former president was chatting with him during the downtime of the four-hour shoot. “You’re just sitting in the Oval Office with President Obama, hearing him talk about stuff,” he says. “He’s got some funny theories.” He relays one of Obama’s most memorable takes: “No one should be using ketchup after age 12. That’s a child’s condiment. It’s just sugar. Use mustard! Use an adult condiment!” Lewis, who joined Higher Ground in 2022 and serves as its head of non-fiction and sports, concurs: “The banter was phenomenal. Being a fly on the wall in that room was incredible.” Despite Schaffer’s praise of his acting chops, Lewis doesn’t think the ex-POTUS will be rushing to add more credits to his IMDb page. “President Obama doesn’t have a great desire to make that career pivot, but it was very fun [to watch him act] and I’m glad it worked out for the show,” Lewis says. “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness” was billed as a seven-episode limited series celebrating the 250th anniversary of America. title: ‘Power Book III: Raising Kanan’ Creator Sascha Penn and Stars Patina Miller and Mekai Curtis on the Deadly Series Finale and ‘Power: Origins’
full_text: Cara Howe SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from the series finale of “Raising Kanan” now streaming on Starz . The final curtain has closed on the hit 1990s-set crime series “ Power Book III: Raising Kanan .” The show has been the origin story of Kanan Stark ( Mekai Curtis ), who, by embracing the very business his drug-queenpin mother, Raquel Thomas (an incomparable Patina Miller ), desperately wanted to keep him away from, becomes the monster who rips his entire family apart. The fifth and final season has not only depicted a young man at odds with his mother, but also his willingness to decimate his own family. Fans of “Power” — Courtney Kemp’s original series — have always known how Kanan’s story ends, but his background has been somewhat of a mystery until now. His story is one rife with terror, pain and a sweltering rage that has usurped everything around him. In “Power,” adult Kanan (Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson) viciously murders his cousin Laverne “Jukebox” Thomas (Anika Noni Rose). Viewers could never reconcile this ending, considering how close the cousins appeared to be. However, series creator Sascha Penn has always promised “a full and complete answer to that question.” “One of the things that’s so interesting about ‘Power’ is the notion of reliable narrators and people’s recollections and how they differ from the fact,” Penn tells Variety . “Something we played with quite a bit across the series is who told the truth. For Ghost [Omari Hardwick] in the original ‘Power,’ the story is always shifting with him in terms of who killed Breeze [Shameik Moore] and who was there, who wasn’t there, who knew?​” Related Stories ‘Obsession’ Star Inde Navarrette Confirms Meeting With ‘X-Men’ Director Jake Schreier and Would Love to Play Mystique Samara Weaving to Play Emma Frost in Marvel's 'X-Men' Reboot In the final moments of the series finale, “Unconditional Love,” that nagging question has finally been answered. In retaliation for Kanan murdering her father Marvin (London Brown), Jukebox (Hailey Kilgrove) kills Raq, the woman who raised her. “Watch until the end of the credits,” Penn says. Popular on Variety ​With this chapter of the “Power” Universe officially over, Variety chats with Penn, Miller and Curtis about the series finale, Raq’s shocking death and how the story will continue in Penn’s upcoming Starz series, “Power: Origins.” Cara Howe Sascha, did you know that this is how the chips would fall for the Thomas family? Sascha Penn : I kind of did. I mean, I didn’t know exactly when all this stuff would happen. I always knew Raq would most likely die in the final episode. That I knew. But I will say this: I did go back and forth quite a bit about that over the years. I think people forget we are telling the origin story of perhaps the most diabolically evil character in the history of the “Power” Universe. So when people are up in arms about Kanan killing Uncle Marvin, I mean, I’m always sort of surprised because it’s like, did you see the character I saw on “Power”? Because that guy was a monster. What was the alternative ending for Raq? Penn: I thought for a little while she could get away like Unique [Joey Bada$$]. I thought that was a possibility. But I’m going to be honest with you, I don’t know that I felt like she deserved that ending, both in terms of the story that we set out to tell, but also in terms of the character. One of the most amazing things about this experience is entirely because of Patina Miller. People have really gravitated toward Raq in the same way they gravitated toward Tony Soprano. Both characters are monstrous in their own ways. Mekai, killing Lou (Malcolm Mays) was an accident for Kanan, but when he kills Marvin, that’s very deliberate. Do you think that’s a pivotal moment of change for him? Mekai Curtis: Absolutely. I think they both are, because one doesn’t necessarily happen without the other. Kanan’s becoming a man. I think everything that he’s run into, everything that he’s been exposed to, everything that he’s learned has led him to this moment. Again, we’re talking about the pursuit of power. We’re talking about the pursuit of being great in this world. And that’s simply what sacrificing Uncle Marv is about for Kanan in that moment. It’s nothing more, nothing less. Kanan, more so than ever, is about his business. He understands all of the seeds that he has sown. After Lou’s death and then again after Marvin is killed, we begin to see glimmers of Raq’s humanity for the first time in a long time. Patina, how did you navigate showcasing this as the walls are closing in on her? Patina Miller: I think her having her little family, which she’s a matriarch of, really meant so much to her. So having the pieces start to fall around her is devastating. She’s been able to work and survive in this world because of the family unit she helped create and protect. To have her brothers, whom she desperately loved — and I know sometimes it might look like she didn’t, but everything she’s done shows that she loved her brothers — to have them gone, the only people she has are her niece and her son. Navigating that was exciting for me. There’s never really time or space for Raq to be vulnerable because of the world she’s in. Raq never gets the opportunity to sit with her feelings because it all comes at a cost. For the first time, you get to see her actually deal with herself, her humanity and the people around her. Cara Howe We have to talk about Shameik Moore’s performance as Breeze, because he’s a wild boy. What was it like working with Shameik? Does Kanan admire him, especially because Breeze is under the impression that they’re actual blood brothers? Curtis: It’s Kanan doing what Kanan does. He’s applying what he’s learned from Raq early on: Get what you can from who you can, hold your information until you very much need it, and just let the cards play out. Kanan is a very observant person, and I know it becomes a topic of discussion for people, especially given how emotionally charged and almost impulsive Kanan seems a lot of the time. But he’s a bit more calculated in why he does those things. One of the quotes that sticks out this season is when Joaquin (Goya Robles) tells Raq that her issue is that she has no boundaries. Do you think that’s true of the character? Miller: Oh, absolutely. I think she’s willing to do whatever, whenever, however. I think she’s so focused that she loses sight of what’s in front of her. In the beginning of this journey, it’s like, “Yeah, Raquel, there’s this woman. She’s in a man’s world, and she’s doing all this for legacy, legacy, legacy.” But then it starts to get a little iffy in the way she uses her power and manipulates the people she loves. She does lose sight of it, but I don’t think it’s because she wants to. I think she still thinks that she’s doing this for a purpose. She’s doing this because she has to. But Joaquin was 100% right about that for sure. Speaking of manipulation, do you think that Raq ever anticipated telling Marvin the truth about who killed Lou? Or was it something she just did as a reaction? Miller: I think it was a reaction. I think that one thing you can know about her is she’s good at keeping a secret. I think she would’ve protected that secret the entire time. But as the stakes grew even higher and she knew Kanan was in a dangerous space and had become an enemy, she needed her brother on her side. She’s always so good at having a card to play. She knows that she can’t do this really, truly without her brother. I don’t think she means to pull it out, but in that moment she saw an opening, and she took it. Before he dies, Marvin accuses Raq of never really caring about him in Lou. How do you think that affects Raq in the final days of her life? Miller: Raq has always been so good at keeping the traumas and all of the hurt at bay. It’s not because she doesn’t want to feel; she knows she doesn’t have the space to feel. I think that it’s a hurtful thing for Marvin to say that because, for her and in my own opinion, it’s like, “I have shown you so many times that I love you. Yes, I’m hard on you, but I went to war twice for you.” There have been so many opportunities where you could have seen if she really hated her brothers. With Lou, she loved him. She really did love him. Obviously, she loves the game, and she loves that they’re in it with her, but she raised [Marvin’s] daughter for him. That’s the ultimate act of love for me. So I think she’s feeling the words, and I think she’s realizing that even though she does love them, they feel this way. And it’s a lot. She’s just trying to put the pieces together and coming to terms with that. It’s devastating. It’s heartbreaking for her in the end, and then to lose him. I think she knows her time is coming. I think she’s ready for it. I think she’s not going to back down from it, which makes it even more devastating. Cara Howe In the penultimate episode, just before Kanan kills Marvin, Marvin tells him that he will eventually meet a lonely, tragic end. It’s something that Juke reiterates when she reveals that she’s killed Raq. Do you think that disturbs him at all? Curtis: A little bit. But at the end of the day, this story is about a mother and son. By the time Juke and Marvin are telling him the things that they’re saying, he already knows it. It’s more of a catharsis for them because they’ve been holding on to it. They’ve been just cleaning up his mess this entire time. London Brown’s performance as Marvin this season is phenomenal; the character development is astounding. Did you always know that Marvin would get this sort of redemption story? Penn: London is an unbelievable talent. I’ve been screaming this for as long as I’ve been doing this: all these actors deserve Emmy nominations. What people don’t really remember at this point is that in Episode 8 of Season 1, Marvin put his hands on his daughter because she’s a lesbian. London and I had many conversations about it, because he really felt like Marvin was irredeemable. He’s like, “Anyone who puts their hands on their daughter for that, how can anyone ever like him again?” And I said to him, “We can do it. I’m telling you we can do it, because here’s the thing about people in general: they have an incredible capacity for forgiveness.” I think that’s what’s happened with the audience: They forgave Marvin. He’s flawed, but he acknowledges his flaws, which, by the way, there aren’t many characters in this show that do that. Sascha, do you think Raq is a good mother? Penn: I’m always sort of intrigued when people talk about Raq as a mother. She’s not a good mother in any way. She uses her son to justify so many awful things. “I’m doing this for you” is the ultimate form of manipulation. During their final conversation, she still needs [Kanan] to say, “I love you.” She still is trying to get that. You see Kanan’s maturation in that moment where he says to her, “No, we’re past all that. That doesn’t matter anymore.” And Raq can’t get past it. She’s a narcissist, and she needs that, and she can’t get it. Patina, do you think Raq anticipated that Juke would take her out? Miller: I don’t think she ever would’ve thought in a million years, just like Marvin would’ve never thought in a million years that Kanan would ever do that to family. That would’ve never crossed her mind, especially for someone she raised, accepted, was there for and loved. I know it’s devastating for her. But even in that split second where she realizes this is happening, there’s nothing she can do about it. And again, she never backs down. Those last few seconds of her going for her gun. I don’t even know if she would’ve ever used it had she gotten to it, but that’s just that thing in her that is never willing to back down. Cara Howe Mekai, when Kanan goes to Raq’s house and sees her body on the floor, what was that like for you? Curtis: It’s devastating, but it is poetic; Raq’s not super innocent. We all love to root for her. She’s the ultimate antihero, but she’s also done her own wrongs. I think as Mekai, I went into that last episode trying to play an overhanging grief, knowing that that was going to happen. Not necessarily having control of it, but understanding what Kanan did and how this was going to come back to him. Raq is one of the most iconic characters I’ve ever seen on television, and her journey has been phenomenal to watch. What have you learned from her these last five seasons? Miller: I think what I’ve learned from her is, honestly, her perseverance. I’ve learned to own my voice. I’ve learned how to walk in my power. I’ve learned to trust myself more, honestly. I gained so much confidence from the very first season through the last episode of season five. I’ve learned to trust my gut, trust my instincts. I’ve learned, even through the craziness and messiness of her relationship, what it truly means to be bonded to someone. Loving my child the way that I do. When I first started the show, I was a new mom, and I just desperately wanted to be a good mother. Raquel’s battling that same thing of just not really knowing how, but wanting to be in her version of being a good mom. I’ve learned to give myself grace, but I think the biggest thing is the confidence to walk into spaces, own them and be yourself. As the narration says, as this series closes, this is in many ways just the beginning for Kanan. We’re going to see him again in “Power: Origins,” the Tommy and Ghost origin story. Can you share anything about what we can expect to see of the character and how this will continue for you? Curtis: Just buckle up. I had a lot of fun putting those 18 episodes together. I said it about “Raising Kanan,” but literal blood, sweat and tears stretched me in ways that I didn’t know were possible. But I’m extremely proud. I feel accomplished and ready for the world to see it. Not just my performance, but the entire show. There’s something different to it. I think with every spinoff that we’ve gotten to do and every spinoff that Sascha’s been a part of, he continues to up the ante. “Origins” is very much up there. We’re constantly pushing the boundary. We’re just trying shit, but I think it all worked out. I’m excited for people to go on that ride with us. Penn: It’s a true privilege to be able to continue the story. First and foremost, tonally the show is very different than “Kanan.” “Kanan,” I think we can agree, is pretty dark. “Origins” is a lot more fun. I sort of crafted it as much more of a two-hander like “48 Hours.” It has a real levity. Not to say there isn’t any darkness, and there is obviously violence and action. We do see Kanan more as the 50 Cent version than the “Raising Kanan” version. But the heart and soul of the show is the relationship between Ghost [Spence Moore] and Tommy [Charlie Mann]. I think this is what the “Power” fan base has really been clamoring for. This is their story. The access point to “Origins” is like, just flip it on. You’re along for the ride. You don’t have to have watched “Power” before. It’s just another incredible ensemble cast we’ve assembled. Again, it is not dark like “Raising Kanan,” and it’s not as glitzy and glamorous as “Power.” It’s somewhere in between. We’re still in South Jamaica. This interview has been edited and condensed. title: Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 5:41pm PT Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season Awards Circuit Podcast: Also on this episode, how 'Widow's Bay' continues to gain momentum — impacting the comedy race. By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest Stanley Tucci on Why His Emmy-Nominated ‘Tucci In Italy’ Is Moving to the United Kingdom Next Season 9 hours ago ‘Baywatch’ Honors Hero 16-Year-Old Lifeguard Ryder Williams During Set Visit (EXCLUSIVE) 14 hours ago ‘Ted Lasso’ Stars on How Women’s Sports Was the Perfect Storyline to Bring Back the Hit Apple TV Show for Season 4 16 hours ago See All Getty Images Italy remains Stanley Tucci ‘s first love. But a man can travel, right? After winning three Emmys for CNN’s “Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy,” followed by two nominations (including this year) for Nat Geo’s “ Tucci in Italy ,” the star is on the move. Tucci tells Variety ‘s Awards Circuit Podcast that he’s currently filming his new season in the United Kingdom, where he lives full time. “I wanted to do the U.K. because I just feel like there’s so much here,” he says. “I’ve been here for almost 15 years now, and London was just voted the best food destination in the world. But I’m not just talking about fancy restaurants and all that. I’m talking about the U.K. as a whole. I think that the produce that’s here — the seafood that’s here, the meat that’s here, the devoted people like these fishermen or lobstermen, or a guy who raises pigs that will be like the best pork you’ll ever eat — that kind of stuff is amazing. And then, really amazing chefs that are devoted to farm to table or farm to fork, I guess is the new expression.” Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Having now done travel shows for a while, Tucci says he considers it “a great honor to meet so many of these people, because they’re just extraordinary. Their devotion to what they do. Amazing chefs and home cooks alike, farmers, cheese makers. I mean, their whole life is invested into this one thing. This singular focus is really so impressive to me.” Popular on Variety Tucci is once again nominated as executive producer and host of “Tucci in Italy,” nominated for outstanding hosted nonfiction series or special. He talks to the Awards Circuit Podcast about what it was like to become a host, the skills he has developed in interviewing everyday people, and whether he’s OK with us calling him “The Tooch.” He also takes our 10 Questions quiz, and looks back at his first time in the pages of Variety. But first, on the Roundtable, Gold Derby editor-in-chief Debra Birnbaum joins us to give her takes on the Emmy race, including how “Widow’s Bay” has become the comedy front-runner. Listen below! “Tucci in Italy” comes at an interesting time for Tucci, who remains busy in front of the camera as well — including this year’s “The Devil Wears Prada 2.” “I’m really happy about having a lot to do, and yet at the same time, at the age of almost 66, I think, ‘how long can I do this?’” he says. “There’s a part of me that wants to spend more time at home, and so I’m trying to orchestrate things so that I can do that without compromising my career. Because there are still things I want to do, stories I want to tell, movies I want to make, plays I want to direct. It’s finding that correct balance.” Hosting a travel show didn’t seem like part of the plan, but Tucci notes that he first came up with the idea of traveling through Italy and breaking it down by region about 20 years ago. “I’d never seen a show like that,” he says. “I brought it up to a few people, and everyone looked at me like I was crazy. And then six or seven years ago, CNN came to me and said, ‘Do you have any ideas for a show?’ And I did. I had two other ideas: One was about refugees and food, and the other was about cancer, finding a balance between standard of care and alternative treatments. No one seemed very keen on either of those. So, and then I said, ‘Oh, I want to go through Italy and break it down region by region.’ And they went, ‘OK!’” So here’s the big question: What’s the most underrated region of Italy that we should check out? “I think Le Marche is a really beautiful region, which is right next to Tuscany. I shouldn’t even be saying this because I know that people will go to it. But it’s a really beautiful region, and it’s not packed with a huge number of tourists. The seaside is really pretty. The food is absolutely wonderful, and it’s not crazy expensive. But it’s gorgeous.” As for hosting, Tucci says there was a learning curve at first. “I was very nervous when I first did it. I thought, ‘What am I doing? I don’t know how to do this.’ I know how to memorize lines, or I know how to improvise, but with an actor, not with a normal person. But now I’m much better at it, and I feel more comfortable.” The secret, he says, is to listen. “If you’re not listening in the scene and responding truthfully, it’s not going to work,” he says. For Tucci’s first time in Variety, it was Oct. 6, 1982, in a review of Broadway’s “The Queen and the Rebels.” Tucci was listed as one of the travelers/soldiers, alongside his pal Campbell Scott. “I had just graduated from college,” he says. “I felt very lucky. I grew up with Campbell, and his mom was doing the play, and she cast us. He had one more year of university to do, I think. We were doing the play in the summer, so it was amazing for me. I understudied a role, and we were cast as extras for all practical purposes, and it was great because it got me my equity card and health insurance. That made a big difference. I was paid $550 a week, and I was in heaven. I thought this is the greatest thing ever. I got an agent, so I had all those things right out of college, SUNY Purchase. That’s a huge thing for an actor starting their career.” 10 QUESTIONS WITH STANLEY TUCCI: 1. Childhood nickname: “Tooch.” 2. Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into it now: “Velveeta.” 3. Go-to karaoke or sing-in-the-shower song: “You don’t want to hear me sing. If you’ll notice in those reviews you spoke of, there’s not a single musical in them, and in a 40-45 year long career, and there’s not a musical. But I sing in the shower, thinking I’m brilliant. Something like ‘Our Love is Here to Stay,’ which is a song that I always sang to my kids when they go to sleep.” 4. Give me an alternate title for your show: “Oh God, you don’t know how long it took us to come up with the simplest title in the book. ‘Tucci Eats Italy’? Just bad.” 5. What’s your secret talent? : “I would say drawing and painting.” 6. Favorite ice cream flavor : “I don’t really eat ice cream. If I had to say, it would be chocolate. It’s so boring. I’m so sorry.” 7. The one item you couldn’t live without : “A knife that I have. That sounds scary, doesn’t it? But no, it’s a chef’s knife.” 8. What TV show in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of? : “Wild Wild West.” 9. Fictional character you most admire : “I really loved doing ‘Captain America.’ I did it like 15,16, years ago, and it was one of the best work experiences I’ve ever had. And I absolutely loved playing that role, even though when I was sent the script, it said, ‘German scientist in his 70s,’ and I was 50. I was like, ‘Oh man, come on!’ But it was so well written, and I just loved it. I just watched it again with my kids the other day.” 10. Your favorite piece of advice : “My acting teacher George Morrison, who passed away a number of years ago, said, ‘go beyond what’s comfortable.’ And the second one is that ‘the undoing of something is as important as the doing of it.’ That was from my father who told me that. And Alberto Giacometti.” Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television.
