title: ‘The Last House’ Ending Breakdown: Why Is the Family Trapped Inside Their Home?
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 5:00pm PT ‘The Last House’ Ending Breakdown: Why Is the Family Trapped Inside Their Home? By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Dwayne Johnson Defends ‘Moana’ After Bad Reviews: ‘Just the Way It Goes’ 12 hours ago ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Director on Their Kinky Rom-Com and Soundtracking the Year’s Bloodiest Scene to Counting Crows 15 hours ago ‘Bridgette Wrona and the Whisper Creek Murders’ Wraps From Little Spark Films; YA Mystery Follows Podcaster Hunting a Serial Killer (EXCLUSIVE) 17 hours ago See All Courtesy Netflix SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “ The Last House ,” out now on Netflix. “The Last House” is a new sci-fi feature that just dropped on Netflix that’s built around a central mystery: What if you and all of your neighbors were locked inside your houses with no option for escape and had no idea why? That’s what Ann (Greta Lee) and Jason (Wagner Moura), along with their two kids, Graham and Ruth (Noah Alexander Sosnowski and Riley Chung), face in this new dystopian tale from screenwriter Matthew Robinson and veteran blockbuster director Louis Leterrier (“Fast X,” “The Incredible Hulk”). Related Stories Samara Weaving to Play Emma Frost in Marvel's 'X-Men' Reboot 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day': Sadie Sink Is [SPOILER]. How Her Role Sets Up Marvel's Next Reboot The film starts on an unexpectedly rainy day, when the family realizes they’re sealed into their house with no way of opening or smashing through the doors or windows. Any attempt is thwarted by a seal seemingly made of rainwater. Popular on Variety Thanks to a well-stocked pantry, the family is able to survive handily as weeks crawl by. Christmas comes and goes, and at points the crew is happy to live the simple life together. But things grow more tense, especially as neighbors that are also sealed in struggle to survive. Although the film doles out answers, there is some economical hand-waving about why the neighborhood has power and running water for so long. And also there’s literally a Chekhov’s Gun, but more on that later. Things hit a tipping point when a neighbor who had been out jogging when everything was sealed runs up to the family’s windows and starts pounding, screaming things “Everyone is dead,” “Don’t let them see you!” and “They’re here, and no help is coming!” She also looks crazed and is carrying a big butcher knife, but is pulled away by wet-looking tentacles which burn bright after they capture the jogger. Things get increasingly bleak, as the family dog’s heart medicine runs out and Jason has to put him out of his misery, and then — in doomsday prepper mode — carves up the body and puts it in the freezer just in case food gets dire. As time goes by, rainfalls grow more sinister, as big monsters claw against the windows if they spot anybody inside, forcing the family to quickly close the curtains. Meanwhile the family is growing increasingly hungry and grumpy with each other, as food runs low with no new signs of escape. But just when it seems like all is lost, Jason comes up with an idea of how to trap animals outside and drag them through the open chimney, while Ann removes the flooring to turn the house into a garden. Unfortunately, the power finally goes out. We jump ahead five years and the house is a full-on farm. The kids are now older and played by different actors (Emma Ho and Gabriel Barbosa). The neighborhood is overgrown, looking like a full-blown forest. While there is plenty of food, everyone looks pretty depressed. Meanwhile, the soil surrounding the house is eroding and the structure is sinking. One day during a big rain, a creature uses water powers to open the door to the house. The family hides from the beast, which looks like a mix between a Cthulhu, an octopus and a big, beefy guy. Beyond causing distress, it appears as if some fluid dripping off the creature instantly deep freezes anything it touches. The alien leaves before it can do much damage, but when it departs the family is still trapped inside. Ruth accidentally tastes saltwater coming from one of the beasts, and they realize that all of the plants and drinking water were poisoned by said saltwater. It also solidifies a theory that perhaps the beasts come from the darkest depths of the sea, instead of the stars. Ruth gets bitten by a ferret that accidentally gets stuck in their food trap, which makes her sick and in need of antibiotics. Jason freaks out and tries to ram his car through the garage door, but it knocks him out and exposes some deeper cracks in the house’s foundation. He then lifts some tile out of the bathroom and realizes it opens up into the sewer drain, which connects the whole neighborhood — including the house of their dentist neighbor who has antibiotics. Ann has to go down into the sewer as she’s small enough to fit, and makes it to the dentist’s house. The inhabitants are long dead, and she grabs the antibiotics, but she’s chased out by a monster, who then realizes that there are humans in their house. The family then works to booby-trap the house “Home Alone”-style, confident that if they can defeat incoming aliens, they can escape out the doors that were opened in the process. The rain starts up again, paired with some nasty-looking cyclones. Water starts rapidly flooding the house, with a creature swimming through, clearly adept at moving underwater as had been predicted. Frantic skirmishes between the family and the beast take place as the house floods, and eventually the invading creature is tangled up in a trap. Jason frees it, hoping it will show the same mercy to them, and it does, letting them into the wilderness. They’re initially surrounded by more creatures, but the beast they helped shooed them away. Their house disintegrates and falls into the ground, and then Ruth — whose kindness to animals ultimately saved them, as it encouraged her father to free that beast — runs to the shoreline. It’s clear that Seattle is now underwater, given that the Space Needle is nearly fully submerged, but the family starts laughing as they go to grab their fishing gear and sail across the now elevated water. The movie ends with Ruth’s narration: “We never saw them again, but we think they’re still out there. After all, it’s their home too.” They finally ask over their boat’s radio if there are any survivors, and get an inquisitive “Hello?” back as the credits roll. Watch the trailer below. title: Amanda Knox Responds To Petition Protesting Her Edinburgh Fringe Show, Says It “Honors Meredith Kercher’s Memory”
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn ‘Blue Bloods’ Alum Will Estes Reprising Role On ‘Boston Blue’: “Welcome (Back) To The Family” Brandi Carlile Postpones UK, European Tour Dates Due To “Personal Circumstances” Amanda Knox Responds To Petition Protesting Her Edinburgh Fringe Show, Says It “Honors Meredith Kercher’s Memory” View All August 7, 2026 4:14pm Amanda Knox attends Hulu's 'The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox' premiere on Aug. 19, 2025 in New York City. Theo Wargo/Getty Images Nearly 20 years after she was falsely accused of killing her roommate, Amanda Knox is still struggling to tell her own story. The author and comedian, who was wrongfully convicted of the 2007 murder of Meredith Kercher, has responded after a petition to cancel her Edinburgh Festival Fringe show Cartwheel surpassed 10,000 signatures. “There is a petition to cancel my show at Edinburgh Festival Fringe. Here is my statement,” she prefaced on Instagram . “ Cartwheel is a show about motherhood, raising a daughter in a world that is unfair and dangerous for women, and what it costs to be the kind of mother who tells her the truth about that. Related Stories News Hat Trick Productions Launches Live Comedy Arm News Leading Comedy Executives Fear Relocation Of Edinburgh TV Fest Would Be "Disaster" For British Talent: "Look At The Number Of People Who Come Every Year From The American Industry" “Neither the author of this petition nor anyone who signed it has seen Cartwheel . The petition contains many false assumptions and completely mischaracterizes the show. Cartwheel honors Meredith Kercher’s memory and calls out the violence that was done to her and to me.” Watch on Deadline Knox continued, “A petition to cancel a show no one has seen, on the grounds of false accusations intended to shame and vilify a wronged woman into silence, is not an argument against Cartwheel . It’s a fairly precise description of what Cartwheel is about and why it deserves to exist. And the Edinburgh Fringe is the perfect place for a show like this. “Many of the Fringe’s most celebrated comedy shows tackle difficult subjects including grief, trauma, mental health, addiction, illness, identity, and politics. Comics rarely treat these experiences lightly or make them the butt of the joke. Instead, they use comedy as a way to explore them, creating space for audiences to engage with complex ideas, connect through shared experience, and find moments of relief, perspective and hope in subjects that might otherwise feel overwhelming,” she wrote. Started by Sally Alington, a former friend and co-worker of Kercher, the Change.org petition said the show “mocks the horrific events surrounding Meredith’s murder and aims to somehow turn this tragedy into entertainment,” calling for Fringe to “withdraw their support for this performance.” Meanwhile, Fringe Society director Tony Lankester told BBC Radio Scotland the festival is “not afraid of controversy,” but the decision ultimately lies with the venue. A rep for the Gilded Balloon Teviot, which will host Cartwheel from Aug. 7-17, said they aim to “provide a platform for a wide range of voices, in line with the Fringe’s longstanding commitment to freedom of expression,” and will allow Knox’s show to continue as scheduled. After Knox was convicted of Kercher’s murder in 2009 and sentenced to 26 years in prison, the conviction was overturned in 2011 and she was fully acquitted in 2015. title: ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 4:00pm PT ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘One Night Only’ Director Will Gluck Cut Out ‘So Much Nudity’ Because People Dislike Sex on Screen: ‘It Takes You Out of the Movie’ 10 hours ago ‘The Odyssey’ Surpasses $1 Billion, Christopher Nolan’s First Movie Since ‘Dark Knight Rises’ to Reach Coveted Box Office Milestone 16 hours ago Natalie Portman, Jenna Ortega Satire ‘The Gallerist’ Lands at Roadside, Vertical 18 hours ago See All ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection “ One Night Only ” director Will Gluck doesn’t want you to overthink it. The filmmaker has been fielding a lot of inquiries about the premise, logic and loopholes of his new movie, a raucous romantic comedy about the one night a year where premarital sex is legal. (Think “The Purge,” but for banging instead of murder.) Monica Barbaro (“A Complete Unknown”) plays Allie, an aspiring singer who channels her talent through embarrassing jingles in drug commercials. Callum Turner (“Eternity”) portrays Owen, a pizza shop owner whose long-term girlfriend decides she wants to sleep with other people on this holy night. The two strangers keep running into each other during 12 hours of messy mayhem in New York City. Related Stories Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Gluck is aware the movie’s setup is sparking more questions — Why does the ban exist in the first place? What happens to people who break the law? How, exactly, is the government even tracking who’s getting it on? — than answers. But he maintains the particulars of this reality aren’t really the point. Popular on Variety “You can’t really describe this movie,” Gluck says. “[The cast] goes on talk shows and spends 80% of the time explaining the rules of the world, and that’s not what the movie is about. We have to just let people see it. That’s the best tool we have, especially for something that’s this crazy.” Gluck, best known for directing 2010s teen classic “Easy A” with Emma Stone, knows all that matters is that people are talking about the film in the first place. Word-of-mouth fueled the success of his last rom-com, 2023’s box office sleeper hit “Anyone But You,” starring Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell. “I learned from my last movie that people are going to discover this and say, ‘Wow, that’s not what I thought it was going to be,’” Gluck says. “You know how the acronym for word-of-mouth is WOM? I’m calling it a WOM-com.” Ahead of opening weekend, the director spoke to Variety about why audiences have become prudish about on-screen sex, his love of putting “cringe” songs in his movies, and why the theatrical rom-com isn’t dead, after all. How did you decide how much backstory to include to set up your premise? I did a lot of thinking about it, a lot of world building. These characters are living this little alternative world that could easily happen. We have to talk about it. But I really wanted the world to live in the background. I didn’t want the movie to be about that. It’s more about how our characters navigate life. What conversations did you have about the origin of the no-sex mandate? Someone asked me “why don’t people just get divorced?” Well, there’s municipal signage very prominently in the movie that says you cannot get divorced unless you were married for one year, plus one day. It’s like when COVID [started], there were rules, and then people started to do other stuff, so then more rules came out, right? That’s what I imagine when this mandate was passed. They had to keep doing amendments to these rules because, yes, the obvious idea would be just get married and divorce. Recent studies have found that Gen Z and Gen Alpha don’t want to see sex on screen . Was that a concern while making this movie? The answer is 100% yes. I went through this on two movies. I have long pages of empirical data about it. The only thing is I don’t think it’s just Gen Z and Gen Alpha. I believe it’s been a societal shift from taking nudity in adult situations and putting them on your phones at home for everybody. Now it’s more of a private, intimate thing that people don’t want to see when they’re in a shared experience. Whenever people now see nudity or very adult situations in a big theater, they get uncomfortable. How does that change your approach as a filmmaker? Once I’ve learned that, which was all through the editing process for my last movie, I applied it to this movie. But even so, I didn’t apply it enough. I cut out so much. There was so much nudity in this movie that we shot on the streets. I felt we needed to show the world that way. As we started to show it to audiences, we felt it takes you out of the movie. You’re engaged in the characters and what’s going on, and then you pan over and there’s two naked people having sex, and you watch the audience … it’s a physical thing. They turn to who they’re with and … the benefits do not nearly outweigh the negatives of it. So we just kept editing it out until we got a balance, and those comments went away. Did you use an intimacy coordinator? So many scenes had extras having sex in the background. Yes, we had an incredible intimacy coordinator. And we cast real-life couples in various stages of relationships. It was never like we met an extra and were like, “you guys are kissing.” It was fun because there were married couples, people who broke up during the movie and people who became couples so they could do that. There are a lot of fun and funny posters and advertisements about “the mandate” and “one night” all around the city. Were those actual props, or were they edited in later? This is all practical. That was the fun part of the world building. We had a huge document with every scene, not only what signage was there, but what graffiti was there and who would be in the background kissing. And the funny thing about the products, I’ve gotta stop reading the internet, but everyone says, “It’s a product placement fiasco. How much money did they make on that?” It was the opposite. We had to beg products to allow us to take them and twist it to the “one night.” Because, as you can imagine, not every corporate America consumer product was into this idea. So when I read stuff, like, “How much money did they get from Dunkin or Durex?” I’m like “Nothing!” So you had to get permission to make the fake ads? Of course. You can photograph anything that’s in the real world, but you can’t take something like Coke ad and say “there’s dirt in it.” We had a big list and it was “no, no, no, no.” And then we were surprised — well, the condom companies didn’t surprise us that they said yes — but Duolingo sure did. That was a shock. I was like, “Really?” So that’s why you have products like Duolingo, Red Bull, Dunkin and Equinox. Every time they would say “yes,” I’m like, “They did?” And then they would have to approve our take on it. What are some of the challenges of filming in New York City? Many times, we had actors in a car, half naked, and you’d have people just walking and staring. We’d say, “Hey, do you mind moving on?” A couple of people said, “No, we’re not going to move.” We were like, “Well, if this really did happen in real life, people would be staring.” So there are a couple scenes where people are looking in the windows. How much of Monica’s character was built around her actually being able to sing? I always rewrite the script completely once I have the actors. Once I cast Monica, I was like, “She has to be a singer.” We talked for a long time, and she does have some stage fright, which is crazy, because she has the best voice. So I just wrote that for her. And I’ve always been obsessed with drug commercials, so it was this great confluence. Did Callum actually learn how to make pizza? Yes, he spent five days at that pizza place being taught how to make pizza. He was really good at it. The one bummer about pizza is it doesn’t look great on film. It’s impossible because pizza gets cold so quickly. During that scene, we were constantly putting out a new fresh pizza. That’s a lesson for me. From now on, I’ll choose a different food that does not congeal that quickly. How quickly did everyone get sick of pizza? You can tell during that scene but Monica and Callum, they ate. They didn’t chew and spit. Because I don’t cut. I just keep rolling. They were both at the end like, “Oh my god.” Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell, your stars from “Anyone But You,” don’t exactly have cameos, but they pop up in funny, unexpected ways. Did you get their permission to include them in the movie? Yes, I did. They were both trying to do cameos, but their schedules didn’t work out. So this was great. Music plays a big part in many of your films. I can’t hear “Pocket Full of Sunshine” without thinking of “Easy A,” and “Unwritten” went viral on TikTok after the release of “Anyone But You.” How do you choose which songs to feature? For the drug commercials, I have a pretty good take on songs that were really popular that people think they hate, but they can’t stop singing. I’m kind of obsessed with those songs, and a lot of my movies have them in it. You’ve mentioned some of them, and I think it’s because people don’t want to admit they like popular music, so they call it cringe or lame. But they’re bangers. After my last movie, if you ever go to any bar or club all over the world, when “Unwritten” comes on, it’s like the biggest banger in the world. It always was, but now for some reason, it’s now OK to be a banger. I love those songs. People often say the theatrical rom-com is dead. What were your takeaways from the box office success of “Anyone But You”? If you’re not a superhero movie or gigantic IP, it’s really hard to cut through. The only way you really can cut through, if at all, is letting the audience do it. No matter how much you market it or tell people what it is, you have to let them see it and tell their friends and family about it, which is scary. If you’re spending all this money on something, you can’t just hope people talk about it. But the key is telling people it’s going to be in theaters for a while. And I think this one is going to be in theaters for a while. title: Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 3:42pm PT Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’ Collins performs Friday night at the Ford in Hollywood as part of her "Sweet Judy Blue Eyes' tour, co-joined by Bruce Cockburn. By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Judy Collins on Doing a Farewell Tour While ‘Having a Lot More Steam in My Engine’: At 87, ‘I’m the Betty White of the Folk Movement’ 10 hours ago Phoebe Bridgers Will Unveil ‘Lost Weekend’ Album in Planetariums in More Than 30 Cities 2 days ago Sienna Spiro on Writing Candidly as a Young Woman, While Being Frank About Adoring Sinatra and Twiggy: ‘Being 20 Is Just Tricky, Period’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Image How sweet — or suite — it still is. Judy Collins is doing a valedictory lap or two around the country on what is billed as a farewell tour, even though, at 87, she’s showing little in the way of weariness about maintaining a full concert schedule or lack of prowess in pulling these shows off. “It’s time” is the fullest explanation she’ll give about why it might be time to think about slowing down her schedule. In the meantime, there is a long way to go on her “Sweet Judy Blue Eyes Farewell Tour 2026-2027,” named for the song pal Stephen Stills wrote to celebrate her almost six decades go. Related Stories Roku City Secrets Revealed: How Long Will Jimothy Last, Why Did the Titanic Get Nixed and Where Exactly Is It Located? Roku Q2 Revenue Up 22% and Net Income Zooms to $164 Million in Huge Beat, Abstains From Providing Outlook Amid Pending Fox Corp. Sale If she thought she’d looked at clouds from multiple angles when she had a top 10 hit with the Joni Mitchell-penned “Both Sides, Now” in 1968, imagine how many more cloud sightings she’s had in her career since then. She changes her sets nightly, but ticketholders for the tour are likely to get a sampling of her most well-known covers — like Stephen Sondheim’s “Send in the Clowns,” Leonard Cohen’s “Suzanne” and the hymn “Amazing Grace” — as well as her self-penned material, as highlighted in her most recent studio release, 2022’s “Spellbound.” Whichever songs she picks, fans won’t likely regret a chance to see her for what may or may not be a local last time. In L.A., she headlines the Ford on Friday night, joined by a fellow monster of folk-rock, Bruce Cockburn. (Openers on some of the other tour dates include such big-name acolytes as Richard Thompson, Amanda Shires, Rosanne Cash and Mary Chapin Carpenter.) Popular on Variety Variety caught up with Collins via Zoom from her New York home as she prepared to fly out for the tour’s west coast swing. Your official farewell tour kicked off July 4, but looking back, you already had had a really busy year. It looks like you’ve done over 35 shows so far in this calendar year, and you’re just getting started. Yeah, we usually do 100 a year, so that’s good. You haven’t yet put an end date on your farewell tour. Does it really feel like this is farewell, or is there some ambiguity as far as how long you might keep going? No, it is a farewell tour. You know, I’ve been doing this for 67 years. I don’t know if anybody took note of that. But I think I’ve done a farewell tour later than most people do. I don’t know anybody to compare it with. But I think a lot of bands and a lot of organizations and groups have done farewell tours, and I think it was appropriate for me to do mine now. And why so? As you said, you’re doing it further along in years than a lot of people who have officially done a last tour. But you have also frequently talked about how you actually enjoy touring. Oh, I do. I love it. But I have a lot of other things in my life that I have to deal with, which is writing a couple of new books, and I have a commitment with a Broadway (producer) with a stage show that I’ve written all the music for. So there are other things, of course, that have to be dealt with. And, it’s time. It feels like you are… I don’t want to say wholly unique, but somewhat unique among performers, in loving being on the road so much. We talk to so many performers who say, “I love the two hours on stage. It’s the other 22 that I can’t deal with.” Yet you’ve said you enjoy the part of touring that other people hate, which is transit of getting from one place to another. I love touring. I love it. And this has something to do with first experiencing being on the road with your father? When I was a little girl, my father was a great entertainer, and it was through him I found my reason to have a career and be doing what I wanna do. He had a a radio career for 30 years, and he also toured at the end of the war. I first was on the road with him when I was a little girl. I was 3, and he was touring with National School Assemblies, and we were up in Butte, Montana when I had my first time on stage. He said, “You want to sing for these nice people?” And I sang “I’ll Be Home for Christmas.” It’s the one I knew. It was April. He said, “Do you want to sing for the people?” And, “do you want to ride in the car?” I said, “I want to do both.” And I love traveling. I love living in New York, but I also get to travel all over. The other day we were with the High Kings, and we were in Duluth, and we had a big show at this huge, wonderful place in the woods [the Big Top Chautauqua]. I was there with Don McLean years ago, and he called me up because he saw that I was gonna be there, and he was reminding me of our show at that wonderful venue. And we were driving in the most beautiful area in Wisconsin, near Lake Superior. I get to see all these places. And I get to ride in planes; I don’t mind planes at all — I love planes. But also we get to drive, and I get to see every tree that’s ever been considered to plant somewhere. I love it. Do I know what they all are? No, because I’m not a botanist. But I love everything that grows. You know, Saturday night I got home, and I raced around and watered all my plants. So your father was a role model for being in show business? I do a lot of things that he did. I tell a lot of jokes. I want to make people laugh. I grew up on the wonderful entertainers who always told jokes. You know, we were babies of that culture. And also, you know, I’m the Betty White of the folk movement. Like Betty White, just in terms of endurance and still being around and enjoying it? Sure. I mean, she certainly kicked off pretty late. And I have a lot more steam… a lot more juice in my engine, I’ll tell you that. Judy Collins Shervin Lainez You’re not bidding farewell because your voice is gone. Everyone still loves to hear you sing. Sometimes we have to wonder if a lot of it is just genetics — that Tony Bennett can sing well into his 90s, and you are doing great well into your 80s, but other people start having voice problems when they hit 70 or even 60. Yeah. Well, the voice is a very tricky thing, and it’s a superb instrument if you can keep it with you. If you can’t… I’ve had my issues with my voice, and I had incredible, unbelievable fortune. First of all, I was given a gift from two people in New York. One was the great teacher who taught me how to sing. By good fortune, I found Max Martley, who was an incredibly gifted teacher, and he taught a lot of people and taught me for 32 years, and I learned what to do. But also, I was an alcoholic. I am an alcoholic but I was drinking for about 20 years. And when I hit 1977, I suddenly couldn’t sing anymore, and I canceled many shows. But then I was lucky because the doctor I was seeing, an ENT doctor named Donald Wiseman, was a genius. And there was no cure for what I had. I had a what’s called hemangioma. People who drink for years get these on their faces, and I was a heavy drinker, but I didn’t get mine on my face — I got it on my vocal cord. It would have stopped me completely forever, and there was no cure at the moment. So Don Wiseman kept at it. He kept saying, “You’re not gonna be singing anyway, so let’s try this.” And it was a process that he did on the vocal cord, and it was removed. I don’t know how miracles happen — I mean, I’m not supposed to be in charge of those — but I got one. And from then on, I went straight back to a clean vocal cord that has been working perfectly ever since. And of course, I know what to do. I mean, I know from Max that I have to remember clarity and phrasing — two things that are my watch words. And so it’s not a mystery really, but it is in terms of technique, because I know exactly what to do, and I also have this clean vocal cord to work with. So I think that what I was given was a gift from the higher power, from whatever, and of course, I immediately… Well, within the next few months, I also stopped drinking, and I’ve been sober for 48 years, which doesn’t hurt. So you got a second chance at life, or your career, in the ’70s… Well, I got another life because I not only stopped drinking, but also, about four days before I went into treatment, I met the man that I was to be living with and married to [Louis Nelson]. We were together for 46 years, and I lost him. Well, I didn’t “lose” him. He died at the end of 2024. So I have gone through this widowhood and the difficulties that come with it. It’s painful, it’s heartbreaking, it’s everything you could think of. But on the other hand, I had all those years. He was an amazing man. He did not have to live in your shadow, with such prominent accomplishments. Among other things, he designed the [mural for the] Korean War Veterans Memorial on the Mall in Washington, D.C., and that’s been very much a part of our lives, too. All of the wonderful people that he was working with, and our trips to D.C., and our engagement with the generals, and all the Koreans, and the people who made it such an extraordinary gift not just to the Koreans, but to us, the Americans. So he was splendid and brilliant and wonderful and all of those things. And I lucked out, that I got to spend all those years with him. For an old hippie like me, I think it’s pretty good luck. Quite a confluence of events, between meeting him and getting your voice repaired… And getting sober. It happened all at the same time, which I think is extraordinary. And I know people that have lost their voices in similar situations to mine. So it is the luck of the draw — I love that old song. The title of this tour is “Sweet Judy Blue Eyes,” a la the Crosby, Stills and Nash song inspired by you, but spelled without the “suite” pun. I think I faintly recall that you might have been mildly embarrassed by Stephen Stills’ song when it came out. But you embraced it enough to make it a tour title this time around. Oh, I wasn’t embarrassed. I mean, that was the greatest compliment he could have given me, and we have been friends ever since. We’ve been friends for close to 60 years, and we still talk, and we still get together. We did a fabulous tour in 2017 and ’18, where we did 115 shows in a year and a half. We just had a ball. We were on the stage for two hours a night together. Each of us had one song that we sang (solo), but everything else was together. He is one of the great guitarists of all time, and playing in that environment with him was such a privilege. I don’t know that he’ll go out again. I don’t know. I see him from time to time. I saw him a couple weeks ago in L.A., and we had a wonderful morning together with his wonderful wife, Kristen, and we always have a lot to say to each other. He came out in March of last year, after Lewis had died, and was on a show that I did at the Town Hall here with a lot of other artists who sang songs either that I’d recorded or that I’d written. And at the end, he came on. We did “Helplessly Hoping,” and then he said, “She married the right guy.” Because he and Lewis were good friends. You change your setlist around a lot, from night to night. But people are generally likely to hear at least one song from your last album, “Spellbound,” which was the first album where you wrote every song on it. So it’s a lot of repertoire to draw upon. Yeah. I like to keep it fresh, for me, but also for the audience, to reach into songs that I haven’t done for a while. And I have a lot. You know, I didn’t start writing songs until I met Leonard Cohen in 1966. And of course, I recorded “Suzanne” immediately. Then he said to me, “I don’t know why you’re not writing your own songs.” So I started. I wrote a song called “Since You Asked,” and I’ve been writing ever since. A couple years ago I came out with a poetry book called “Sometimes It’s Heaven.” And the reason was that my husband had dared me to write every day, in 2017. I had said, “Well, now it’s a new year. I’ll start a new notebook…” And he said, “Why don’t you write 365 songs or pieces of songs, and then you’ll have a whole book of poetry,” which I did. It came out a year and a half ago. And I harvested all of “Spellbound” from all of that writing. I should have called it “365 Days,” but I didn’t. You must imagine Leonard Cohen would have been proud? Oh, yes. Oh, he would be so happy. You know, he was sort of like having an angel on your side. We were friends for a long time. He used to call me and read me verses of “Hallelujah” — he wrote about 40 — and he would say, “Do you like it?” And I said, “Well, it’s not me that is gonna have to like it. You’re gonna have to like it.” He finally narrowed it down, but it wasn’t easy. Is there any song you’re most proud of adding to our musical vocabulary? Well, I’ve written a lot of songs that people seem to like to sing. I just found out that one of the young rock and rollers in the ’80s recorded “My Father.” I went to the doctor this morning, and my doctor’s nurse is a fiend about collecting and listening to rock bands, and she found this rock band —. I don’t remember the name — who recorded “My Father” in the ’80s, and I was so happy to hear about that. [The version of “My Father” referred to was likely This Mortal Coil’s.] Sometimes you’ve done Dylan’s “Masters of War” in concert, although not lately. which You’ve said you’re a big fan of Heather Cox Richardson and people like that. Do you feel political at this moment in time? Oh, gosh. I don’t know what to do about it all the time, but I do. And yeah, Heather Cox Richardson is my favorite. I met her with Lewis, my husband, and they just went nuts. We went out to a big event with my brother Mike, who died five days after Lewis did. My brother had had a terrible, cancer of the mouth for five years. It’s a horrible disease. But we happened to have met Heather Cox Richardson in Illinois somewhere, and it was a good meeting and such a good time that we had with her. So, yeah, I think she’s wonderful. I told her, “I’m trying to be a Lincoln Republican” — trying to follow her, course. You know, I think we all do what we can. I have something in my hip pocket, though, that I do almost every night. I have had two dozen roses in a vase under the piano for decades now. They never go anywhere; they just sit there. And starting this past Jan. 1, I was in England, there they were, the flowers. So when we finished singing “Amazing Grace,” I took the flowers out of the vase, and I started singing “Where Have All the Flowers Gone?” and I distributed the flowers to the audience. It has continued to be a very wonderful moment. And it is my political statement of the night, and it works wonders. Going back to this being a farewell tour, you mentioned at some point that there may be some kind of “encore” shows after the tour ends… Well, I don’t know about that. I just know that I’m on a farewell tour, and I like being here. And billing it as such helps people to know, “OK, take advantage of this while you can. “ Well, that’s true. title: Keen Ruffalo Never Intended to Get Into the Family Business
full_text: × Skip to main content Keen Ruffalo stars in the new Prime Video series ‘Sterling Point.’ Photography by Evan Mulling Keen Ruffalo never planned to get into acting. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, the now-25-year-old was in school for fashion design. Understandably, he wanted to find his own path instead of jumping into acting like his father Mark Ruffalo. But the pandemic changed his plans. He found himself not knowing what he’d do next with his life. “I was depressed as most people were during COVID and needed to figure out what to do,” Ruffalo tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent Zoom. He realized that acting had brought his father joy, so he decided to explore why. Instead of looking for roles, Ruffalo opted to study the craft first. He instantly fell in love. “I went to so many goddamn conservatories,” he says. Related Stories TV How Ella Rubin Went From Being a Briefcase-Wielding 11-Year-Old to the Star of 'Sterling Point' TV Inside 'Sterling Point': Why Megan Park's YA Series Trades Tired Tropes for a Refreshing Dose of Realism But Ruffalo was waiting for one specific OK. “Finally, my dad saw a play that I did, and he was like, ‘You might be ready now,’” he recalls. “He gave me the A-OK to go out into the world.” Getting out into the world was clearly the right move, as the actor’s releasing two projects in Prime Video’s Sterling Point and the Green Day comedy Nimrods . In Sterling Point , he plays Connor, the twin of the show’s main character Annie, played by Ella Rubin. Given his father’s long career, one would assume that Ruffalo basically grew up around it. But he found his childhood to be quite removed from Hollywood, both in the figurative and literal sense, having grown up on a farm in upstate New York. He didn’t even realize that what his dad did for work was different from his neighbor’s dad, a dairy farmer, until he was a bit older. “It wasn’t until someone came up to me and was like, ‘Hey, can you have your dad sign this Hulk Funko Pop for me?’ [that I realized],” he says. “I was like, ‘No, you’re horribly mean to me.’” “I really didn’t understand the gravity of it all until a little bit later in life, and even then I was kept pretty far away from it all,” he says. However, working with the Sterling Point cast allowed the actor to collaborate with a host of other young people also newer to the industry. “It’s such a cool thing to be doing with them because we’re all at this weird point [in our careers],” he says. “Being able to work with such talented creators and artists at that point in their career where we’re all still getting the hang of it a little bit is something that’s really special and not very common.” In a conversation with THR , the the actor digs into Sterling Point , the best advice he’s received, his favorite non-acting activities and why he doesn’t want to get behind the camera (for now). You said you initially weren’t planning to get into acting. Is it more rewarding to figure it out on your own that you want to be there? Definitely. My parents were never ones to make us do anything or, especially, impose any of their own ideas for what our career paths might be, which I appreciated a lot. Maybe [they were] a little bit more enthusiastic about playing soccer, but they were kind of like, “Yeah, do whatever.” Sunrise Coigney, Mark Ruffalo and Keen Ruffalo at the 2015 Toronto Film Festival. Harold Feng/Getty Images for LiveNationStudios What’s the best piece of advice you’ve received? It doesn’t have to be from your dad. God, I don’t know. I feel like it’s a hard one because so many different people say so much. A lot of time people ask me for advice, which I’m like, “Dude, I’ve been here just as long as you have. I don’t know what you want.” I think the thing that always kept me going is hearing about … and this is actually from my dad, so sorry. I’m not breaking the mold here, apparently. You’ve got a good source for information. I get it. Yeah, resident expert, but he was always talking about how he had to do so many auditions before he even got into a room, where they even gave him a chance. Keeping that in mind and not beating myself up over not getting something that I was really excited for, or knowing that eventually something will come around, [and] you just really need to keep up until you get there and don’t drive yourself crazy. I think that’s a really hard part about it. Is there anything in the world you feel you can’t live without? Probably my bed. I love a pillow. I think I couldn’t go without that one pillow. Music is another one that’s super important because that’s always shifting just throughout life. What do you listen to these days? I’ve listened to a lot of Midwest emo punk recently. I feel like that’s a little bit of an embarrassing one to admit. There’s one song that I really liked recently, I’ll tell you because honestly, I think that they deserve more eyes on them. It’s “Will They Blame Me If You Go Disappearing?” by Hail the Sun. It is so good. That is the best emo title song as well. It’s always a full sentence. It is a full sentence question mark at the end. Correct grammar. It’s a really cool song that I’ve been jamming out to a lot recently. I love it. But definitely wouldn’t show it to many people. I’ll go to a photo shoot or something and they’ll ask me if there’s a song I want to put on. I say no whatever they want. Keen Ruffalo at the Dior Cruise 2027 show. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for Christian Dior Are you still interested in fashion? Fashion’s something that I’ve kind of been around for a long time. My mom used to be a model, so she’s always been outspoken about fashion. It was jewelry-making that I actually was really into. I used to hammer, fire, the whole thing. That’s my medium in that, but I’m definitely still interested. It’s just a cool thing seeing how it’s always changing. I don’t know. I went to my first fashion show. How was that? That was a trip. It was really cool. It was the Dior show. I was just enjoying the show, and I looked around and everyone had their phone out. I thought, “Oh, wait, I should be doing this too.” I’ve never experienced anything like that. Being invited to an event was surprising. I don’t know. I’m like, why do they want me there? I’m just a farm boy. How old were you when you started making jewelry? That’s quite an intensive hobby to just pick up. I’ve always been a bit of a hands-on person. I didn’t do great in school — I’m ADHD, dyslexic — [and] always had a hard time there, but I liked making stuff. I think the first time I ever did anything like that was maybe at a summer camp. They told us we were going to make leaves out of sheet metal. I really enjoyed that, and then kept going back to this person that ran that little class and doing more stuff with them. [I’ve] probably been doing metal working since, God, maybe I was like eight or seven. Then I started building boats for a while there. I’m also an ADHD kid, and every few weeks I wanted a new hobby. It seems like you actually stuck with yours. I’ve given up on plenty of hobbies. But I’ve built a few canoes. They were usable? Yeah, I sold them. Wow. You’ve lived a lot of lives. I’ve done a bunch of different things. I think they all kind of fall into the creative sphere of it all. I wish I was good at music. I wish I could play a guitar or something. That’d be cool. Keen Ruffalo as Connor in Sterling Point. Courtesy of Prime Is there anything that people would be surprised to know about you? I feel like building boats is a pretty random one. I don’t know my months. That’s another one that I find weird. In what way? What do you mean? I know next month’s August because I keep being told that, and the show’s coming out next month. I don’t know what the next month after that is though. I don’t know what happened there, but something got lost in translation. The worst time management. I can also relate to time management, but at least you have a device with a calendar at your fingertips. At this point, I’m doing it out of the spite. I’m like, “It gets cold at one point and then it warms back up. That’s all.” That is very funny. Yeah, you are definitely the first person to tell me that. Maybe an elementary school kid won’t know their months, but 25 years old, doesn’t know his months. It’s pretty out there. How are you feeling with the release of Sterling Point and Nimrods and people seeing them? It’s definitely anxiety-inducing, I’d say. It’s hard because I’ve grown up seeing that a little bit. When I got older, I’d be able to go to premieres and stuff and see that. Both of my things are coming out within 10 days of each other. I’m getting my money’s worth out of my PR team right now, which I’m sure they appreciate. I’m excited and anxious. I hope that people can get what they need from these projects and that they enjoy it. So much of this job is balancing making the thing and going out there and telling people to see it. It sounds like you saw it at least a bit from a distance growing up. Have you figured out the balance? I feel like [my dad’s] a bad example for that. He’s a very polarizing person. ( Laughs .) I’d definitely say a lot of our cast is like, “We need to do what? I don’t have TikTok.” Do I almost just not make a TikTok at this point out of standing on business with that one? I already have a panic attack every time I open up Instagram. I’m like, “Oh God, do I have to post today?” We’ll see. It’s definitely a part of it, and at the end of the day, you get opportunities through doing press. I’m amazed that you guys, for example, reached out and wanted to have this meeting. I’m just very honored and feel lucky to be here. Keen Ruffalo attends the premiere for Sterling Point . Jason Mendez/Getty Images for Prime Video You’re coming to terms with that still then, I guess? Yeah. I’m like, “The other guy should be here not me.” Imposter syndrome. That’s pretty common for people in their 20s. I imagine it’s maybe a bit more when you are doing something that your father is quite famous for? Yes. There’s definitely been a lot of trying to navigate and cope around that. Obviously, I’m very proud of him and love my parents. I’m just trying to not disappoint them in the long term and stand on my own at the end of the day. What kind of roles are you into? Any audition that comes across, I usually do because I just enjoy it. But I love period pieces. I love dramas. I went to drama school, so give me something sad and depressing. I’ll eat that up. I guess also indie projects. I think it’s really important to do as many smaller productions as possible, especially just in this day and age where a lot of creatives aren’t getting that opportunity because they’re smaller. Any way I can use my platform to get something that I think needs the voice to get made, that’s kind of the end goal of all of this. I want to take European jobs from European actors. Put me in a medieval project. I’ll learn the accent. But I think movies are where my head’s at. Doing shows is great, but after doing a long show like this, I want to meet these different people. I want to be able to give a voice to many different people, not just Connor. Do you have any interest in the filmmaking part of it? Oh, boy. I think that there are a lot more people who deserve that more than me, who’ve put a lot more time into learning how to do that. Maybe someday I’d love to. I have a production company, and my entire thing is if I’m going to make a project, I’m going to do it with two known people and everyone else is unknown. title: Spencer Pratt Joins the Chat on the Federal Film and Television Tax Incentive
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All August 7, 2026 3:17pm Spencer Pratt at the 2025 American Music Awards held at the Fontainebleau Las Vegas on May 26, 2025, in Las Vegas, Nevada. Getty Images The federal film and television tax credit has a new lobbyist, it seems. Reality TV star and former L.A. mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt on Friday posted on social media that he had recently met President Donald Trump to advocate for the tax incentive. This legislative effort has been stop-and-start for well over a year. “Working with the President on a 25% FEDERAL film tax credit to bring back Hollywood,” the former The Hills star said, sharing images of himself and the president speaking at the Trump National Golf Course Los Angeles. After making a few accusations about California’s film commissioner and Attorney General Rob Bonta, he added, “The adults in the room are actually trying to repatriate the most quintessential American industry. I’m committed to saving Hollywood, and I’m very grateful for the President’s remarkable generosity and focus on this issue.” Related Stories TV The Man Behind David Lynch, Kathryn Bigelow and 'Beverly Hills, 90210' Gets His Moment at Locarno TV John Oliver Says Taco Bell Has the Moral High Ground Over Trump Administration Amid "Explosive Diarrhea" Parasite Crisis The Hollywood Reporter has reached out to the White House for comment. A representative for Pratt declined to comment further. A large coalition of industry advocates and organizations, from the Motion Picture Association to industry unions to President Trump’s “special ambassador” to Hollywood Jon Voight, has long been championing the idea of a stackable incentive for films and TV series produced in the U.S. Several sources in this cohort reached on Friday said they didn’t believe Pratt was working in coalition with the larger group. “Although we haven’t had conversations with Spencer or his people, we appreciate the support of anyone who has the President’s ear that can help push this initiative forward,” said SP Media Group president Scott Karol, who is part of Voight’s team advocating for the credit. “At the end of the day, what matters is getting a meaningful federal incentive, and bringing good paying jobs back to America.” The idea has bipartisan support, as THR previously wrote , with Rep. Laura Friedman of California and Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia emerging as key backers of the potential legislation in the House. Sen. Adam Schiff has long been a proponent in the Senate. It’s unclear, however, whether Pratt is advocating for the same kind of credit as they are. After becoming an outspoken critic of politicians’ responses to the 2025 Palisades Fire, Pratt ran for L.A. mayor earlier in the year on a populist platform, gaining the support of President Trump along the way. After his defeat, Pratt has emerged as a vocal detractor of a lawsuit from 12 state attorneys general aiming to block the $111 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. He has claimed that California Gov. Gavin Newsom and attorney general Bonta are attempting to “cripple two of the greatest film studios of all time over politics.” (Newsom has not weighed in on the suit publicly yet, though a Wall Street Journal report in early August suggested he was concerned about the impact on state employment if the merger were blocked.) Now, it appears, the TV personality has turned his attention to legislative efforts to boost the entertainment industry. Said Pratt in his social media post, “He [Trump] is very passionate about revitalizing the entertainment industry and we will not let Canada, or the U.K. or Budapest steal our lunch anymore.” Pratt’s advocacy for a federal tax credit arrives after Paramount Skydance head David Ellison made headlines for traveling to Washington to lobby Republicans on the idea. Can the involvement of Pratt, a registered Republican, and other conservatives finally enthuse the president on the long-gestating idea? Only time will tell. In the meantime, below Pratt’s post on Instagram, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt posted two raising hands emojis. Aug. 7, 6:16 p.m. Updated with Scott Karol statement. THR

title: Flo Anthony Dies: Groundbreaking Columnist & TV Personality Was 74
full_text: Skip to main content By Erik Pedersen Erik Pedersen Managing Editor More Stories By Erik 2026 Premiere Dates For New & Returning Series On Broadcast, Streaming & Cable Movie Academy Foundation Board Re-Elects Kim Taylor-Coleman As President; Other Officers & Members Set Critics Choice Super Awards Geek Out Over ‘The Boys,’ ‘Widow’s Bay,’ ‘Superman,’ ‘Obsession,’ ‘Good Boy’ Dog & More View All August 7, 2026 2:51pm Flo Anthony in 2007 Getty Images Florence “Flo” Anthony, a trailblazing entertainment journalist, author and TV and radio personality who broke a number of barriers for women of color, died August 6 of cancer. She was 74. Jack Hirsch, biographer of Anthony’s husband, Olympic and pro boxing champ Michael Spinks, confirmed the news to Anthony’s longtime publication New York Amsterdam News. Related Stories Obituaries 2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Obituaries 2025 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries Born on March 4, 1952, in Ann Arbor, Michigan, Anthony began her career as a publicist for athletes including Muhammad Ali and fellow champion boxers including Spinks and Larry Holmes, working with the latter from 1982-85 including his reign as heavyweight champion. She began working as a journalist during the 1980s and made a name the following decade as a scoop-making celebrity reporter and becoming the first woman staffer at the New York Post ‘s sports and entertainment department and its famous Page Six. She aspired to be a sports reporter and started at the Post as an agate clerk in 1986 before moving to the entertainment department. She detailed her seven-year Post experience in a 2013 interview with the website Urban Bridgez: “After a while, they said, ‘You flunked the job,’ and I was like. ‘What do you mean I flunked?’ But it was the thing of being the agate clerk, you had to do a lot, and I would be there all night till like 5 in the morning. So they was like. ‘Don’t worry, we see you have a masters degree in fine arts. We’re moving you to the entertainment department.’ I went to the entertainment department kicking and screaming. They said, ‘Look it’s a day job and pays more money, so why are you upset?’ So I went from the first African American woman in the sports department to the first African American woman in the entertainment department.” Anthony went on to become a familiar face to viewers of talk shows and celebrity-themed entertainment news programs. She appeared on shows hosted by the likes of Geraldo Rivera, Sally Jessy Raphael, Maury Povich, Joan Rivers, Ricki Lakeand many others and was a regular contributor and sometimes co-host on E!’s The Gossip Show during its entire 1993-98 run. She also did episodes of such programs as Inside Edition, Entertainment Tonight , E! True Hollywood Story, Most Shocking Celebrity Moments and Most Annoying People and was a frequent contributor to TV One’s Life After, Unsung and Unsung Hollywood. Her popular weekly column Go with the Flo launched early this century in New York Amsterdam News and in syndication. She also had a nationally syndicated radio segment called “Gossip to Go With Flo” and another called “ Flo Anthony ’s Big Apple Buzz” and was in the magazine game, serving as publisher and editor-in-chief of Black Noir and as editor-in-chief of Black Elegance . In that 2013 Urban Bridgez interview, she also discussed the definition of a journalist. “Well, a journalist is someone who actually looks for a real story,” Anthony said. “Not just picking something up off of a blog and not just being some wildcat person with a blog, but someone looking for a real story. Someone who researches the story, talks to people regarding the story and also a journalist is someone who breaks stories.” Anthony also was a novelist, penning the books Keeping Secrets, Telling Lies, Deadly Stuff Players, One Last Deadly Play and Last Call for a Deadly Diva . She began dating Spinks in 1987, around the time he was the IBF heavyweight champion before losing the title to Mike Tyson. They married early this year. She and Hirsch co-authored Michael “Jinx” Spinks: An Authorized Biography . full_text: Aug 7, 2026 2:28pm PT Olivia Rodrigo Debuts ‘Pretty Sad’ Songs at Sweltering Brooklyn Surprise Show: Concert Review By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Olivia Rodrigo Debuts ‘Pretty Sad’ Songs at Sweltering Brooklyn Surprise Show: Concert Review 11 hours ago Peter Katsis, Veteran Manager for Backstreet Boys, Korn, Jane’s Addiction and More, Dies at 69 1 day ago Music Industry Moves: Alicia Keys Signs With CAA in All Areas; SONA’s Emerging Songwriter Award Nominations Now Open 2 days ago See All (Photo by Xavi Torrent/Getty Images) The announcement dropped on a pulverizingly humid Thursday afternoon in New York City: just a few hours later, an Olivia Rodrigo surprise gig would take place at Brooklyn’s intimate, 1,100-capacity venue Warsaw. The expected mad dash for tickets — only available at the venue’s box office — ensued, with fans lining up in heat that was technically 91 degrees but with a “real feel” of 105. But of course, the venue was packed long before the 8 p.m. showtime, even though it was just as hot inside. Rodrigo, clad in a red flowered schoolgirl dress and black go-go boots, dove in at the deep end, starting the set ambitiously with the album’s first single, “Drop Dead” — a challenging song to sing, with its upper-register chorus that offers few opportunities to take a breath — but she pulled it off with ease. “We’re going to be playing a lot of songs from my new album for this first time,” she said, and promptly obliged with three more tracks from “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” concluding with the Wet Leg-esque “My Way.” Popular on Variety Her five-piece band was razor-sharp — they’ve played a number of concerts this year, from the Primavera Festival in Spain and “Saturday Night Live” to a surprise cameo with the Smashing Pumpkins at Lollapalooza last weekend — but apart from an “Austin City Limits” taping last weekend, this was indeed the first time most of the eight new songs have been performed for a concert audience. A man is seemingly trapped inside a Netflix billboard above Sunset Boulevard. The potential traffic-stopping (or perhaps even accident-causing) sight is a marketing stunt for the streamer’s new thriller The Last House . The unidentified actor entered the installation — which is crafted to look like the front window of a house — on Thursday and will leave on Saturday, Aug. 8. From Netflix: “He’ll attempt to maintain a sense of normalcy over extended periods of time while ‘stuck’ in his elevated, enclosed set 30 feet above the ground at Selma Avenue and Sunset Blvd — communicating with commuters and passersby below via whiteboard as an eerie nod to the family’s own isolation in the film.” Related Stories TV 'My Life with the Walter Boys' Love Triangle Resolved: Showrunner, Cast Weigh in on Long Awaited Pairing, "Brutal" Outcome and What's Next Movies 'The Last House' Review: Greta Lee and Wagner Moura in a Claustrophobic Netflix Thriller Most Effective While the Threat Remains Unknown A video, below, shows the man looking like he’s eating cereal and rather confused and miserable. title: Virginie Efira’s Love for Cinema and Locarno Has No Limits — Even If Her Mic Does
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 2:02pm Virginie Efira at Locarno 2026 on her way to receiving the Leopard Club Award Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press Belgian-born actress Virginie Efira ( All of a Sudden , Parallel Tales , Benedetta , Paris Memories ) took the stage in the central Piazza Grande square at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival on Friday evening to receive this year’s Leopard Club Award . “It is truly a joy, a privilege and an immense honor for me to be here with you to receive this award,” she said in French in front of a huge crowd in the Italian-speaking part of Switzerland, before adding: “I sincerely apologize for only speaking French. Do most people understand?” The crowd’s answer was a loud “yes.” Related Stories Movies 'I Is Another' Review: Claes Bang Plays Himmler's Masseur in Weighty Meditation on a WWII Footnote Lifestyle As Tom Holland and Zendaya Rule the Box Office, We Look at Their Reported Wedding Bash at the Decadent Beaverbrook Hotel She continued with praise for the Locarno festival. “I also want to say, and I feel this very strongly when I see you all here in this square, … that Locarno is perhaps the festival with the greatest faith in the audience,” Efira offered. “The idea [is] that we, as viewers — and I share this belief, like you — are all hungry for films that resonate with us, that move us, that innovate, that offer us something greater, and that we are not finite entities with predictable desires, that we want to be surprised. And Locarno truly has that trust in the audience, and that warms my heart.” She continued: “The Locarno Film Festival is truly avant-garde. It discovers artists, it looks at a cinema that is being invented, and that is extremely important.” Efira also got emotional, sharing: “I think it’s the first time I’ve received an award like this. I’ve received awards before, at Cannes, for example, but not a recognition like this for several films and for a career. It touches me deeply.” But the star emphasized that film is about more than one actor. “I share this award with the public who love films, and I also share it with directors, who are true creators,” Efira told the Locarno crowd. “Because for an actor, this award is a very heavy burden. An actor on their own isn’t much. It’s truly a collective profession. And to achieve something that might have some merit, you need a vision.” Virginie Efira Efira then namechecked various directors she has collaborated with, such as Ryusuke Hamaguchi, Justine Triet, Rebecca Zlotowski and Valérie Donzelli. “On your own, you’re not much,” Efira concluded. “And without the audience, you’re nothing at all. So, thank you for your curiosity.” While at the Swiss festival, Efira will present Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden ( Soudain ), for which she won the Palme for best actress at Cannes and for which she learned to act partly in Japanese. With that film and Asghar Farhadi’s Parallel Tales , Efira pulled double duty in this year’s Cannes competition, winning the best actress honor together with her All of a Sudden co-star Tao Okamoto. When she mentioned that people in the square can see that film in Locarno on Saturday, her microphone cut out for a few seconds, but the star quickly decided to simply continue talking without amplification, just more loudly. When the mic started working again seconds later, she said to laughs: “Oh, it works, great!” Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro had introduced the star, also in French, full of pride. “It is an incredible honor to welcome Virginie Efira, an incomparable artist,” he said, also praising her for “always remaining true to herself.” And he concluded: “Virginie Efira embodies the modernity of cinema.” After Efira received her honor, it was time for the world premiere of I Is Another ( Ich Ist ein Anderer ), written and directed by Felix Randau and starring Claes Bang ( The Square , Bad Sisters , Home ) and Valerie Pachner ( The Stories , Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore , Four Minus Three ), which tells the story of Nazi Heinrich Himmler ‘s former massage therapist. The creative team briefly discussed their film and shared their excitement about being on stage in front of a crowded square full of film lovers. Shared Bang: “I must say: This looks much better than in photos. People, you are amazing! Thank you for coming!” The crowd erupted into applause and cheers before the star added: “This is so pretty and beautiful and wonderful.” THR

full_text: Florence “Flo” Anthony, the pioneering celebrity journalist who broke barriers at the New York Post’s Page Six and became a defining voice in African American entertainment journalism, has died. She was 74. Jack Hirsch, biographer for her husband, boxing legend Michael Spinks, confirmed that she died early Thursday, Aug. 6. The two had worked together on Michael “Jinx” Spinks: An Authorized Biography , which was released in March. He said that she recently disclosed to him that she was battling cancer. Her weekly “ Go With The Flo ” column became a fixture in The New York Amsterdam News dating back to 2001, as well as in publications including the Philadelphia Sunday Sun and the Columbus Times . She also contributed entertainment news to the New York Daily News , served as publisher and editor-in-chief of Black Noir magazine, and acted as editor-in-chief of Black Elegance magazine. CNN entertainment journalist Lisa Respers France posted her reaction on social media upon learning of Anthony’s passing, saying in part: “As a Black woman who covers pop culture, I am deeply indebted to Florence ‘Flo’ Anthony, a syndicated columnist and author who did more than just cover gossip. She was so important to the culture.” A woman of firsts Anthony was known to walk into newsrooms and departments whose doors had once been barricaded against people of color—and particularly against African American women. She entered spaces where few people looked like her, where her presence alone challenged entrenched ideas about who could report the news, break a story, command a television screen, or become a trusted voice on celebrity culture. She became the first woman to work in the sports department of the New York Post and the first African American to work in the newspaper’s entertainment and world‑renowned Page Six departments, according to her own account of her career. She also made history as the first African American woman to write a column for a supermarket tabloid, penning “Eye on the Stars” for the National Examiner . For an African American woman rising through the overwhelmingly white, male, and notoriously insular world of tabloid journalism, these achievements were not merely promotions, but breaches in a wall. Before becoming one of America’s most recognizable celebrity journalists and media personalities, Flo worked in public relations as a publicist for some of boxing’s most formidable figures, including Spinks, whom she began dating in 1987 and married in January 2026; Muhammad Ali; Larry Holmes; Butch Lewis; Mike McCallum; Matthew Saad Muhammad; Saoul Mamby; and Eddie Mustafa Muhammad. Her publicity work gave her a deep understanding of the relationship between journalists, publicists, and public figures, allowing her to fight for a client’s visibility long before she sat on the other side of the desk. Many publicists owe some portion of their careers to Anthony, with a number of young representatives securing an early placement because she answered their call, opened their email, or recognized the potential in a story. A graduate of Howard University, Anthony initially came to New York with dreams of becoming an actress and also worked as a teacher. Her work with talent manager Tobe Gibson eventually expanded into publicity, sportswriting, and a position as an agate clerk in the New York Post’s sports department. From there, she began a historic ascent through sports, entertainment, and celebrity journalism. Legendary journalist Over the course of her career, she reported hundreds of exclusives, including the marriages of Mike Tyson and Robin Givens, Alec Baldwin and Kim Basinger, and John McEnroe and Tatum O’Neal, as well as the news that Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman were adopting. Flo did not regard gossip journalism as the careless recycling of rumors. To her, a gossip columnist was a reporter who broke stories—and she took the responsibility of getting those stories right seriously. Her influence expanded far beyond print. During the 1990s, she became a familiar and authoritative presence on daytime television, appearing on shows hosted by Joan Rivers, Ricki Lake, Rolonda Watts, Geraldo Rivera, Sally Jessy Raphael, Maury Povich, Leeza Gibbons, Tempestt Bledsoe, Bertice Berry, Vicki Lawrence, and others. She appeared on Court TV, CNN, MSNBC, Fox News Channel, and HLN, and contributed to entertainment‑news programs including “Inside Edition,” “The Insider,” and “Entertainment Tonight.” For six seasons, she appeared as a contributor and later a co‑host on E! Entertainment Television’s “The Gossip Show,” and was featured in numerous installments of “E! True Hollywood Story.” She became a regular contributor to TV One’s “Unsung,” “Unsung Hollywood,” and “Life After.” Her television work placed an authoritative African American woman at the center of national conversations about celebrity, scandal, and popular culture at a time when such visibility remained far too rare. Through her company, Dottie Media Group LLC, Flo extended her voice into syndicated radio with “Gossip on the Go With Flo” and “Flo Anthony’s Big Apple Buzz,” which aired in approximately 20 markets and introduced millions of listeners to her combination of insider knowledge, brisk reporting, and unmistakable personality. At the Amsterdam News, she was more than a byline. She was family. Flo was also the author of four novels: “Keeping Secrets, Telling Lies,” “Deadly Stuff Players,” “One Last Deadly Play,” and “Last Call for a Deadly Diva.” The books transformed decades of observing fame, ambition, deception, and power into fiction, bringing the practiced instincts of a journalist to the suspense and intrigue of a novelist. “I’ve broken in roads that will never be broken in again,” Anthony said in a 2013 interview with Urbanbridgez.com . “So if I never wrote another sentence or got on radio again in life or got on TV, I would miss it yes but I feel I’ve done a lot of what God put me on this earth to do.” — with reporting from AmNews contributor Jason Gonzalez. He was 80. The veteran actor was found dead in his Bronx residence by a neighbor on August 1. Pastore’s manager had not heard from him for three days, but according to a close friend, the actor’s driver had spoken to him on the phone Friday night. The death is believed to be from natural causes and is not being investigated by the medical examiner. It has been confirmed that he passed away on August 1. While working as a limo driver, he met Matt and Kevin Dillon, who went to see him in a community play he was doing, and The Entourage star Kevin helped him get his first break. After minor parts in early 1990s movies such as Goodfellas, Carlito’s Way and Men of Respect , Pastore rose to prominence with his roles in the 1995 feature The Jerky Boys: The Movie and the 1996 HBO TV movie Gotti , in which he appeared alongside future Sopranos co-stars Tony Sirico, Frank Vincent and Dominic Chianese. It was David Chase’s 1999 drama The Sopranos that gave Pastore his signature role, Big Pussy, Tony Soprano’s (James Gandolfini) longtime best friend and mob enforcer-turned-FBI Informant whose murder became one of the Emmy-winning series’ most memorable scenes. ‘The Sopranos’ Season 1 cast, from left: Tony Sirico, Steven Van Zandt, James Gandolfini, Michael Imperioli and Vincent Pastore Pastore’s extensive feature credits also include Mickey Blue Eyes, Two Family House, Riding in Cars with Boys, Witness to the Mob, Deuces Wild, Mafia!, Serving Sara, This Thing of Ours, Shark Tale, Bachelor Party Vegas, Once Upon a Time in Brooklyn, Money Train, A Brooklyn State of Mind, The Deli, Spinning Gold and Guy Ritchie’s Revolver. In TV, Pastore was a frequent guest star on Law & Order and had major roles on The Practice, Son of the Beach, Queens Supreme, Hawaii Five-0, Wu-Tang: An American Saga, the daytime drama One Life to Live and the miniseries The Last Don II . He most recently was a series regular on Gravesend and guest starred on Yellowjackets . During the 2000s, Pastore was a fixture on reality television with appearances on Celebrity Apprentice, Celebrity Family Feud, Dancing with the Stars, Shark Tank and Celebrity Fit Club . He also hosted The Wiseguy Show on SiriusXM and performed with the band The Gangster Squad. “Vinny was a great guy, he would help anyone and was very charitable,” Pastore’s longtime manager Bob McGowan said.
